item.content:encoded:
金正恩对中国的奇特访问

中国 | 战友 2026年10月29日

朝鲜领导人金正恩很少出国访问。因此，他于10月24日对与中国接壤的中国城市丹东的突然访问值得关注。在向俄罗斯靠拢四年（向俄派遣军队和补给以支持乌克兰战争）之后，金正恩正在重建与中国的关系。他可能还在为与美国展开新一轮外交做准备，甚至可能在11月与总统唐纳德·特朗普会面。

金正恩此次访问的官方目的是纪念中国于1950年出兵支持朝鲜共产主义北方的朝鲜战争。中国和朝鲜正在大力宣扬战时的团结。今年是两国“友谊”条约——一项共同防御条约——签订65周年。尽管如此，金正恩在中国土地上如此高调地承认中国的战争努力仍然罕见。他对两国关系的评价也异常热情，称双边关系是“鲜血凝成的”。

金正恩在没有会见中国领导人习近平的情况下出现在中国，也很不寻常。两人曾在朝鲜首都平壤会面——今年6月，习近平时隔七年后首次访问平壤。此前，两人于2025年在北京举行过峰会。然而，这一次，习近平正忙于筹备中共早就安排好的中央委员会会议，该会议于10月26日在北京开幕。他派出了在中国领导层中排名第四的王沪宁代为会见。金正恩自上台以来此前五次访华，每次都与习近平当面会谈。

金正恩通常乘坐他的私人装甲列车跨越边境，该列车也可以在中国铁轨上行驶。但这一次，他乘坐一辆梅赛德斯·迈巴赫豪华轿车，驶过鸭绿江上的一座大桥——鸭绿江是分隔两国的河流。这座桥于2014年建成，是中国早先推动扩大跨境交通联系的一部分。但在金正恩处决了曾主导该项目的舅舅（后者后来被指控策划政变，并被认为与中国过于亲近）之后，大桥的开通一再推迟。它终于在10月15日通车。

金正恩的访问和大桥的开通似乎都是为了缓解中国对俄罗斯在朝鲜影响力日益增长的担忧。中国占朝鲜官方全球贸易的90%以上。但金正恩与俄罗斯领导人弗拉基米尔·普京近来关系日益密切。作为对 troops 和武器的交换，俄罗斯向金正恩提供了燃料、食品和军事技术。两国于2024年签署了共同防御条约。它们还扩展了各自的跨境基础设施，包括一座于9月开通的公路桥。

作为回应，习近平公开淡化了其对朝鲜核野心的担忧。与此同时，中国一直在升级与朝鲜的交通联系，并放松对跨境贸易的限制。今年前九个月，官方双边贸易额达到23亿美元，高于去年同期的19亿美元。王沪宁表示，新桥将有助于“扩大人员往来和贸易合作”。

最耐人寻味的是，金正恩的访问可能意在协调其与美国的外交。特朗普在第一任期与金正恩会晤三次，希望达成一项终结朝鲜核计划的协议。在其中的两次会晤之前，金正恩都曾在几周前访问中国，与习近平会谈。美国总统曾表示愿意再次与金正恩会面，可能是在11月中旬于中国南方城市深圳举行的亚太领导人峰会期间。美国官员此后试图打消这个想法，称会晤不太可能。但一些中国政府顾问表示，习近平对此很感兴趣。他希望重新确立自己的影响力，并确保中国在特朗普与金正恩可能达成的任何协议中拥有发言权。通过让 rival 大国相互抗衡，金正恩再次将一手弱牌打得出色。■

订阅者可以注册我们的新周刊通讯 Drum Tower，以了解世界如何看待中国——以及中国如何看待世界。

item.title: China loves to rank its cities. The government wants it to stop
item.description:
China

China | Closing ranks Oct 29th 2026 A scandal is turning over tables in China. Each year apparatchiks in cities and counties across the country battle one another for coveted municipal rankings. The league tables, which are published by media and consulting firms, declare winners and losers in t...
item.content:encoded:
China loves to rank its cities. The government wants it to stop

China | Closing ranks

Oct 29th 2026

A scandal is turning over tables in China. Each year apparatchiks in cities and counties across the country battle one another for coveted municipal rankings. The league tables, which are published by media and consulting firms, declare winners and losers in the race for development and attractiveness of living. The rise and fall of many county-level cadres can be traced to a “100 strong counties” list published for the past decade, until this year.

The central government wants to end such competition. New rules have banned organisations from creating data-based rankings or awarding special titles to cities and towns without permission.

Blame officials in Haicheng, a city in the rust-belt north-east, who in 2025 appeared to be so good at their jobs that they leapt from well outside the 100 strongest counties to 91st on the list. It was revealed this year that they had in fact paid CCID, the consulting firm behind the tables, around 5m yuan ($750,000) for the boost. The disclosure caused uproar among ambitious bureaucrats. One frustrated statistician in Hubei province called the incident China’s newest form of corruption.

Municipal pecking orders have long been a useful, if unofficial, way of understanding a country with around 700 cities and close to 3,000 counties. Since the late 1990s most have received an informal “tier” status. The first tier—Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai and Shenzhen—has always been clear. Things grow murky at the fifth and sixth. Property developers have used these rankings to gauge real-estate values. The central government has never officially recognised them, although it does refer to city tiers in some property-market data.

Consulting firms have made a business out of rankings. A city-research unit at Yicai, a media group, began evaluating and scoring hundreds of cities in 2016. The same year CCID started issuing its top-counties list. Others have published scorecards focused on specific industries or administrative geographies. One online media outfit publishes a list of city districts with the strongest economies. State-backed groups also participate. The China National Institute of Standardisation (CNIS), for example, issues a report that ranks cities on natural beauty and culture, among other things.

The most closely watched list has been Yicai’s, which tracks 337 cities. It has used metrics such as economic competitiveness, intercity mobility, industrial strength, consumer spending and even nightlife to devise scores for each city. Among these is the “new-first-tier” ranking, a list of China’s 15 most promising second-tier cities. Officials often cite such rankings as a mark of success. Those in Haicheng made sure to highlight their incredible achievements in the county’s annual work report for 2025.

The crackdown on rankings might make it more difficult to figure out who is up and who is down. CCID appears to have stopped posting its “100 strong counties” list after the Haicheng debacle. CNIS posts its ranking in October; it had not released one at the time of reporting. Yicai has continued to publish a wide range of information on Chinese cities this year but has stopped assigning them clear rankings. These are still easy to create with the data Yicai provides, wonks point out.

Perhaps it is a good time to phase out city rankings. Ma Liang, a professor at Renmin University in Beijing, has observed that city officials have started experiencing “ranking anxiety”. With economic growth slowing considerably since scoring began, a property crisis sapping local finances and a perpetual anti-corruption campaign upending careers, it is one less thing for them to fret over. ■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: China’s most successful Astroturf operation: grassroots football
item.description:
China

China | Chaguan Oct 29th 2026 ON A COOL autumn night, a man dressed as Guan Yu, a legendary general from 1,800 years ago, mounted his black steed and charged around a stadium. From the stands 26,000 fans erupted in cheers—and then thunderous chants for their football team: “Yiyang must win!” Nea...
item.content:encoded:
China’s most successful Astroturf operation: grassroots football

China | Chaguan

Oct 29th 2026

ON A COOL autumn night, a man dressed as Guan Yu, a legendary general from 1,800 years ago, mounted his black steed and charged around a stadium. From the stands 26,000 fans erupted in cheers—and then thunderous chants for their football team: “Yiyang must win!” Nearly two hours later Yiyang had lost, 1-0, to their stronger opponents from Changsha, the capital of Hunan province. Yiyang’s players, their bright orange jerseys muddy and socks torn from the hard-fought match, could not hold back tears.

Welcome to the spectacle, and the emotion, of the grassroots provincial football leagues sweeping across China. “Xiangchao (the Hunan league) is better than the World Cup,” goes one local joke. The skills are—put politely—uneven, with lots of missed passes, fluffed shots and, in the Yiyang match, a goal review that took 11 excruciating minutes. But the passion is real, more so than that surrounding China’s perennially inept national team.

The city-versus-city amateur competitions began only in spring 2025, starting in Jiangsu, and have inspired copycats in about 20 other provinces. Officials see the leagues chiefly as economic catalysts. Their most striking impact, though, has been social. Against the backdrop of a sluggish economy, they have given people something to cheer, and with all the devotion and irrationality of sports fans anywhere. “It’s been a morale booster for us,” says a sponsor of the Yiyang team.

A few hours before kick-off, the plaza outside the Yiyang stadium had a carnival atmosphere. Stalls sold spicy soup, stinky tofu, a mashed tea drink and other local delights. The biggest queues were for giveaways, including jars of Hunanese chilli relish. Superfans gathered early to bang on drums, wave oversize flags and belt out their chants. They were a good-natured bunch, joking with fans of the opposing side and wrapping Chaguan in a team scarf. Cheerleaders warmed up for their half-time performance; in keeping with the family atmosphere of the whole event, they were clad in ankle-length Chinese opera-style robes.

In the streets around the stadium, the penumbra of China’s property downturn is visible in closed restaurants, half-finished buildings and unoccupied flats. A business partner of the Hunan league says it was created in part to revive economic activity. Officials had tried several things, from night markets to concerts. Nothing worked as well as football, he says. It drew spectators, young and old, as well as out-of-towners. With domestic tourism bemoaned as homogeneous and predictable—cities offer similar pedestrian streets, similar trinkets, similar virtual-reality experiences—there is something to be said for the drama and uncertainty of sport. The inaugural season of the Hunan league brought a Cinderella story when Yongzhou, much poorer than Changsha, clawed its way to the championship.

The matches also tap into a vein of local pride. Decades of migration for work have torn many Chinese from their home towns. Now that they are richer, people are searching for new forms of meaning. Football is one way to reconnect with and express their local identity. “It’s your own family out there,” says Mr Zhang, a convenience-store clerk. Though he worked in Changsha for many years, he could never bring himself to support the capital. “Speaking frankly, Changsha is like a landlord. They have far too many advantages.” In her social-media videos, Zhou Meimei, an influencer from Yiyang, emphasises the value of friendly exchanges between Hunan’s cities. Yiyang, often overlooked by other Hunanese, can show off its hospitable culture to visiting fans, she says. Yet she is competitive, too. “We all want to win because as locals we want our hometown to earn honour,” she says.

The provincial leagues may help football’s image in China. At the professional level, the China Super League is seen as hopelessly corrupt, marred by match-fixing scandals. The provincial leagues have a purity about them. “There’s no money in these games, just people struggling to win,” says one fan at the Yiyang match. Some hope the triumph of these leagues will radiate upwards to the national team, which has not reached a World Cup since 2002. But the provincial leagues come far too late in players’ development to feed into the national programme. Nevertheless, rekindled enthusiasm may entice more young people to play.

Rules are in place to keep the provincial leagues resolutely amateur and local. In Hunan, for example, each team must have at least three high-school students on the pitch at all times. All players must have ties to their city, such as a hukou (household registration). Governments also keep ticket prices down. In Yiyang, seats were just 9.9 yuan ($1.50); nearly 90,000 people had entered the ticket lottery. When scalpers muscled in, authorities introduced facial-recognition turnstiles, ensuring that original ticket recipients could not sell their seats.

For all their grassroots feel, the leagues are mostly run from the top down: bureaucrats organise the matches, vet the entertainment and manage the commercial deals. Their charm depends on that hand staying light. Much as Chinese cities compete to attract investments, they may also start treating league standings as a performance metric. Languishing at the bottom of the table could reflect poorly on a city’s organisational abilities, so the pressure to lure better players or spend more on training is likely to grow.

Money is starting to wend its way into the local leagues. In Jiangsu, sponsors now include Heineken, Coca-Cola and Adidas. In Yiyang, by contrast, one of the main sponsors was a hometown producer of packets of little dried fish seasoned with a fiery sauce. Fans queued for samples of the spicy minnows and for photos with the CEO, a local success story. For now, the small fry are thriving. But the big fish are circling. ■

item.title: America’s decisive voters are its most recent arrivals
item.description:
United States

United States | In full swing Oct 29th 2026 THE DEATH knell for Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign first sounded in Loudoun County, Virginia. Home to affluent voters, one-quarter of whom are of Asian descent, the county had plumped decisively for Joe Biden in 2020. When it was reported, early...
item.content:encoded:
America’s decisive voters are its most recent arrivals

United States | In full swing

Oct 29th 2026

THE DEATH knell for Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign first sounded in Loudoun County, Virginia. Home to affluent voters, one-quarter of whom are of Asian descent, the county had plumped decisively for Joe Biden in 2020. When it was reported, early on election night in 2024, that Ms Harris had won by 16 points compared with Mr Biden’s 25, pundits wondered if there had been a glitch.

The county may now move left once more. At an early-voting centre, volunteers recently handed out sample ballots in Hindi. Arjun, a man in his 50s, described a case of “buyer’s remorse” after backing Donald Trump two years ago. “Everything he said was a lie,” he explained. Outside Patel Brothers, a bustling supermarket, one woman said she will vote for Democrats because Mr Trump’s cuts have gutted care for her disabled child. Other former Trump supporters said they were repelled by the Iran war, high prices, cuts to visas, cruel deportations and reductions in the federal workforce. “A lot of my friends lost their jobs,” said Mohammed, an architect.

Mr Trump’s declining popularity in Loudoun in some ways mirrors trends across the country: nationally, his net approval rating is -27. But these swings, towards Mr Trump two years ago and away from him since then, are not distributed evenly across America. Instead, they have been concentrated in states and districts that are geographically disparate but share a striking demographic similarity: they have large shares of Asian or Latino voters.

Democrats and Republicans alike have too often conflated demography with destiny. For the left, the growing ranks of non-white voters seemed to ease the need to win over culturally conservative whites, while Republicans have feared that immigrants would secure lasting Democratic power. Indeed, the share of eligible voters who are Latino has risen from 9% to 16% in the past 20 years, while the share of Asian-Americans has risen from 3% to 5%. But both sides were wrong. America’s fastest-growing ethnicities are also its most politically open-minded. That gives the country’s newest Americans disproportionate sway in determining its direction.

In this country of immigrants, recent arrivals have shaped party politics throughout its history. The latest wave began after 1965, when immigration quotas were lifted and people began arriving once more, mainly from Latin America and Asia. They did not become rigid partisans. Exit polls showed that Ronald Reagan won 37% of Hispanics in 1980 (he described them as Republicans who “don’t know it yet”), and George W. Bush won a robust 44% in 2004. In the 1990s the Republican Party fared even better with Asians, winning them outright in 1992 and 1996.

It was not until 2012, when exit polls found Barack Obama winning 73% of Asian-Americans and 71% of Latinos, that strategists started seeing these groups as reliable Democrats. “With New Support Base, Obama Doesn’t Need Right-Leaning Whites Anymore”, read one headline in the Atlantic in 2013. Mr Trump’s victory in 2016 seemed to vindicate the idea that Republicans should run up their numbers with white voters, rather than reach out to ethnic minorities.

Yet despite Mr Trump’s often racist rhetoric, his share of the Hispanic and Asian vote inched up in 2020, a trend that accelerated in 2024, when he won 40% of Asian voters and 46% of Hispanic ones (see chart 1). In that election, according to the Co-operative Election Study (CES) at Harvard University, Asians and Latinos made up 14% of voters, but comprised 24% of those who voted for a presidential candidate from one party in 2020 and a different party four years later. That does not make them the biggest bloc of swing voters in absolute terms: non-Hispanic white voters still outnumbered them in 2024, comprising 59% of switchers. But their rejection of strict partisanship, growing numbers and reasons for changing parties are what gives them particular clout.

Even in 2012, when Mr Obama won more than 70% of Asians and Latinos, only 13% and 27% of them identified as “strong” Democrats, according to polling for The Economist by YouGov. Hispanic voters, as well as Asians, stand out for their heterodox positions, agreeing with Democrats on some topics and Republicans on others. Analysing a series of policy questions in the CES, The Economist found that around 34% of Latinos and 30% of Asians hold views which are either moderate or combine left- and right-leaning positions, compared with only 20% of white voters. Latino and Asian respondents’ views on any single issue are less likely to predict how they will respond on another subject. For example, Asians are unusually supportive of both regulating pollution and work requirements for government benefits. Hispanics are more likely than other Americans to back a ban on abortion as well as cancelling student debt.

In part, these combinations of views are a product of diverse cultural traditions between these groups and within them, as well as a range of income levels (see chart 2). They are also a reminder that newcomers do not fit neatly in pre-existing categories. Naturalised citizens are overwhelmingly Hispanic or Asian. Just 9% of Asians and one-third of Hispanics have two native-born parents (compared with 90% of whites and 77% of blacks), making them less likely to inherit a partisan identity.

For these voters the culture wars, which bind a large and growing share of white voters to a particular party, are less important. Economic issues are paramount. In polling for The Economist by YouGov in September and October, the share of respondents listing consumer prices or “jobs and the economy” as their most important issue was 57% for both Asian-Americans and Latinos, compared with 50% for black respondents and 45% for white ones.

That reflects the broader priorities of Latino and Asian-American voters. They spend more time working than the average American. Latinos are more than twice as likely as whites to start a business; Asian-Americans spend more time in school. “Even if you’re not yourself an immigrant, but you’re descended from them, you’re in this country to work hard and get ahead, and that means that economic considerations come ahead of so much else,” says Carlos Odio, a researcher who specialises in surveying Latinos. As Ruben Gallego, a Democratic senator, put it last year, “every Latino man wants a big-ass truck”, often described affectionately as la troquita.

All this set up Latino and Asian-American voters as the perfect swing group in 2024, when prices were the dominant issue. Latinos were particularly exposed to the spike in petrol prices in 2022 owing to their higher-than-average spending on cars, trucks and fuel. Later, in 2023 and 2024, the effect of inflation shifted to housing costs; that disproportionately affected Asian-Americans, who spend more on housing than other groups. This year it is Mr Trump’s turn to feel their wrath.

According to a series of large-sample polls of likely voters conducted for the Argument, a digital news company, Democrats’ margin over Republicans has risen by 17 percentage points among Hispanics and 14 among Asians since 2024, compared with ten for white voters and five for black ones. And although poll cross-tabs can be prone to errors, statewide elections since Mr Trump’s inauguration show the same trend. In gubernatorial elections in New Jersey and Virginia last year and California’s all-party House primaries in June, Democrats’ biggest gains relative to the presidential vote of 2024 were in precincts or districts with their states’ highest concentrations of Asians and Latinos.

Their discontent will play a crucial role in the midterms. Republicans in Texas pushed through a gerrymander that could net the party up to five seats in the House—if only Mr Trump could hold on to his gains in largely Hispanic south Texas. Instead, our forecasting model favours Democrats in three of these districts, and makes Republicans only narrow favourites in two more. In total, Latinos and Asian-Americans represent a larger than average share of voters in 28 battleground House races (see map).

Latinos and Asian-Americans will bring their political heft to high-profile statewide races, too. Combined, they make up 36% of the electorate in Texas and 24% in Florida, the two largest Trump-voting states. Democrats trail by just a few points in both states’ gubernatorial contests, thanks largely to leads among Hispanics of 12 points in Florida and 27 points in Texas. For the Senate, an upset in Florida is unlikely. But James Talarico is up by two points overall and 33 points among Latinos in his bid to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Texas since 1988.

“I’ve spent most of my career telling white, well-intentioned political consultants and candidates that Latinos aren’t a monolith,” says Chuck Rocha, a Democratic political consultant. He now says the opposite: “they’re all monolithically pissed.” Democrats are hammering the president for turbocharging consumer prices by imposing tariffs and beginning a war.

In California’s dusty, agricultural Central Valley, Randy Villegas, a Democrat, is running to unseat David Valadao, a moderate Republican in a district whose voters are two-thirds Hispanic. “I want you to raise your hand”, Mr Villegas said at a rally in Bakersfield, “if you or someone you love drives across the border to Tijuana to get cheaper prescription drugs, cheaper dental care, cheaper health care.” Hands shot up all around the room.

In addition to the economy, this year immigration looms large. Voters in both groups, who by definition have already become citizens, generally support border enforcement and take a moderate view on immigration. But they see the president’s tactics as going too far. In Florida María Elvira Salazar, a Miami-area Republican incumbent facing a tough Democratic challenger, ran an ad in September addressed to Mr Trump in which she said that “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

In early 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents targeted California’s agricultural heartland. They are once again roaming the area ahead of the midterms. In Delano, a farm town that swung towards Mr Trump by 15 points in 2024, shop signs are mostly in Spanish and residents often greet each other with a friendly “buenos días”. Now the streets are quiet and many stores remain shuttered. “I just don’t love what’s happening with immigration,” says Griselda Aguilar, a 34-year-old mother who backed Mr Trump two years ago but attended Mr Villegas’s rally. “The way it’s been handled is inhumane.”

In the waning days of the campaign, the White House—far from easing its rhetoric on immigrants—is playing it up. J.D. Vance, the vice-president, has touted Mr Trump’s deportation campaign and wants a radical overhaul of visas for skilled workers. In Montana on October 26th, he offered adulation for Americans who “homesteaded this land” and “buried their own kin” in the state’s “beautiful soil”. Mr Trump has repeatedly warned, without evidence, that illegal voting by non-citizens will threaten the elections’ integrity.

This obsession is hardly welcoming to Asian or Latino voters, nor does it address their main concern: the economy. If they help secure victory for Democrats, the party may assume that supporters are “coming home”. The lesson of recent years, however, is that neither party should take these voters for granted. Even as more Asians and Latinos swing left, fewer identify themselves as Democrats than in 2024.

“The fact that we view it as so peculiar that Latinos are moving by 20 points is the sign of what’s wrong,” says Mike Madrid, author of “The Latino Century”. Among other constituencies, “nobody moves despite pandemic and war and recession and depression,” he says. “If people do a bad job, you fire them. Latinos are the only group doing that.” ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

美国 | 多米诺骨牌可能如何倒下 2026年10月29日 当一股不可阻挡的力量遇上不可撼动的物体，总有一方必须让步。在唐纳德·特朗普第二任期的大部分时间里，专家们一直认为，这个物体——共和党看似坚不可摧的参议院版图——比那股力量——民主党在全国民调中的领先优势——更占上风。去年，领先的预测机构萨巴托的水晶球将共和党称为“强有力的热门方”，认为他们能保住参议院多数席位，并将阿拉斯加州、爱荷华州和堪萨斯州列为“安全”的红色席位。直到今年6月，该机构仍发现足够多的竞选至少“倾向于”共和党，足以让该党控制参议院。如今，距离中期选举不到一周，传统观点认为那股力量已经占据上风。水晶球的最新更新称民主党“...
item.content:encoded:
我们对中期选举结果的预测

美国 | 多米诺骨牌可能如何倒下 2026年10月29日 当一股不可阻挡的力量遇上不可撼动的物体，总有一方必须让步。在唐纳德·特朗普第二任期的大部分时间里，专家们一直认为，这个物体——共和党看似坚不可摧的参议院版图——比那股力量——民主党在全国民调中的领先优势——更占上风。去年，领先的预测机构萨巴托的水晶球将共和党称为“强有力的热门方”，认为他们能保住参议院多数席位，并将阿拉斯加州、爱荷华州和堪萨斯州列为“安全”的红色席位。直到今年6月，该机构仍发现足够多的竞选至少“倾向于”共和党，足以让该党控制参议院。如今，距离中期选举不到一周，传统观点认为那股力量已经占据上风。水晶球的最新更新称民主党“在参议院争夺战中略有优势”，而博彩市场认为民主党有67%的概率翻转参议院。美国最著名的定量选举预测者内特·西尔弗给民主党的概率是76%。但《经济学人》自己的预测模型更为谨慎，认为参议院易手的概率仅为54%。 这种分歧的主要来源是我们的模型有意违背了一条常见的预测准则：你不应试图预测民调误差的方向。尽管“总体选票”调查——询问受访者他们计划支持哪个政党竞选国会议员——有着令人印象深刻的准确性记录，但它们也有明显的过度夸大倾向：浪潮选举的结果通常不如宣传的那样声势浩大。例如，在2006年中期选举前夕，民主党在这些民调中平均领先13个百分点，而他们在全国众议院投票中的最终优势仅为7个百分点。当全国民调失准时，这种误差通常也会出现在各州的民调中。今年民主党的优势在总体选票上约为8.5个百分点，没有2006年那么极端。尽管如此，根据历史数据，我们的模型预测全国各地的民调将高估该党的优势约一个百分点。这一差距在历史上倾向于民主党的州较小，但在共和党州较大——而要想控制参议院，民主党至少需要赢得两个特朗普在2024年以两位数优势获胜的州。另一个潜在因素是筹款。总体而言，民主党参议院候选人在各自州从个人捐赠者（每人上限3500美元）那里获得的捐款远多于对手。许多预测模型对此赋予了很大权重。然而，自特朗普首次就职以来的每一次选举中，民主党参议院候选人在这一类别中的筹款总额也超过了共和党人。这并未转化为超越民调的选举表现。因此，我们的模型将每位候选人的筹款额与其所在政党的平均水平进行比较。这有助于共和党在爱荷华州等地的前景，我们在那里认可了他们的候选人勉强获得微弱财务优势。相对于共识，我们的模型对民主党在阿拉斯加州的前景最为悲观。博彩市场认为玛丽·佩尔托拉以69%的概率击败共和党现任议员丹·沙利文，而我们的模型显示这是一场51比49的竞争，沙利文领先。佩尔托拉还可能因她的团队在选票上安插搅局候选人的指控而受影响，这一争议很可能主导竞选的最后一周。尽管如此，我们的模型仍然明显看好民主党在足够多的州（包括缅因州、密歇根州、北卡罗来纳州和俄亥俄州）获胜，从而赢得50个参议院席位。模型还给予他们在另外两个州（阿拉斯加州和得克萨斯州）五五开的机会，这两个州可能是决定第51个多数席位的州。重要的是，我们的模型给予民主党95%的概率赢得众议院的控制权，这将使他们能够否决特朗普的议程，并对他的政府发起调查。赢得参议院将使他们也能够阻止他的司法提名人选。参议院议员任期为六年，其构成也将强烈影响特朗普的继任者（将在两年后当选）能否实施党派议程。展望2028年之后，民主党的第52个席位可能与其第51个席位同样重要。而他们目前有一条合理的路径赢得远超52个席位。他们的候选人在堪萨斯州、爱荷华州甚至南卡罗来纳州的民调中并驾齐驱——南卡罗来纳州的长期共和党现任议员林赛·格雷厄姆于7月去世，由他的妹妹、政治新手达琳接替。10月28日，美国最著名的民调团队《纽约时报》和锡耶纳学院报告称南卡罗来纳州势均力敌，而特朗普两年前在该州以18个百分点的优势获胜。民主党在这些州都是小幅劣势方。然而，如果这些多米诺骨牌中哪怕有一块倒下，他们很可能受益于全国性的民调误差，从而提高其他骨牌也随之倒下的几率。如果内布拉斯加州的独立候选人丹·奥斯本——他发誓如果当选不与任何一党组成党团——转而加入民主党，我们给予该党15%的概率至少控制55个席位。即使在2006年，当总体选票严重高估民主党优势时，该党仍然成功翻转了六个参议院席位并确保了多数席位。 ■ 通过《美国简报》——我们的每日通讯，快速分析最重要的政治新闻，以及《制衡》——一份每周评论，审视美国民主的状况和选民关心的问题——来掌握美国政治的最新动态。

item.content:encoded:
中期选举可能重塑美国政治，其影响远超国会

美国 | 下层投票的忧郁 2026年10月29日

最近一个周六的早晨，在威斯康星州格林代尔，50人聚集在一栋简朴的牧场式房屋外，准备为民主党敲门拉票。前州党主席本·威克勒在对人群讲话时强调了他们任务的重要性。民主党有机会终结该州16年来的共和党主导地位。

威斯康星并非民主党唯一关注州。尽管争夺国会的斗争在全国范围内最受关注，但民主党也有机会夺取多个州政府的控制权。共和党在23个州拥有“三连胜”——即同时控制州议会两院和州长职位。民主党有16个。如果蓝色浪潮足够大，民主党可以创造六个新的“三连胜”，包括威斯康星州，并打破共和党的几个“三连胜”。

这种转变的影响将极为深远。州政府在堕胎、教育、医疗保健、税收和劳动法等问题上拥有巨大权力。它们还帮助决定选举规则和国会选区的划分，从而影响华盛顿的权力平衡。拥有“三连胜”的政党可以相对轻松地推行其议程。

威斯康星就是一个典型例子。尽管民主党人托尼·埃弗斯于2019年成为州长，但威斯康星仍保留着其共和党前任斯科特·沃克在“三连胜”执政期间颁布的大量保守法律。沃克削弱了工会，允许私营部门雇员在不支付费用的情况下享受集体谈判的好处。他还大幅削减了公共部门工人的集体谈判权。他的政府抵制提高最低工资（目前仅为每小时7.25美元），并拒绝根据奥巴马医改扩大医疗补助计划。离任前，沃克签署立法削弱了继任者的行政权力，使埃弗斯更难扭转政策方向。

州党主席德文·雷米克表示，凭借“三连胜”，民主党可以撤销沃克的“破坏遗产”。他们还可能将大麻合法化，将堕胎权写入州法律，并终止该州的学校代金券制度。2023年一场司法选举让州最高法院获得自由派多数席位后，他们的前景有所改善。最高法院推翻了威斯康星的选举地图，促使共和党议员批准由埃弗斯绘制的新地图，而不是冒险接受法院可能强加的更不利版本。在新地图下，民主党在2024年取得了重大进展。他们现在只需翻转州众议院五个席位和州参议院两个席位。

在其他地方，实现民主党“三连胜”的路径各不相同。在亚利桑那州，与威斯康星一样，民主党需要翻转州议会两院，才能创造该党60多年来的首次“三连胜”。在密歇根州、明尼苏达州和宾夕法尼亚州，只需一个议院易手。在内华达州，关键竞争是一场势均力敌的州长竞选。这六个州恰好也都是总统大选的战场州。如果2028年总统选举像前两次一样激烈，这些州议会的控制权可能至关重要。

■ 通过我们的每日通讯《美国简报》（快速分析最重要政治新闻）和每周专栏《制衡》（审视美国民主状况及对选民重要的问题），随时了解美国政治动态。

item.title: The winners and losers of Trumponomics
item.description:
United States

United States | MAGA transfer Oct 29th 2026 ALL POPULISTS promise much to the working man, but Donald Trump predicted a golden age. Just before the election in 2024, he told voters they were days away from “the best jobs, the biggest paycheques and the brightest economic future the world has eve...
item.content:encoded:
The winners and losers of Trumponomics

United States | MAGA transfer

Oct 29th 2026

ALL POPULISTS promise much to the working man, but Donald Trump predicted a golden age. Just before the election in 2024, he told voters they were days away from “the best jobs, the biggest paycheques and the brightest economic future the world has ever seen”.  His unorthodox blend of tariffs, tax cuts and deportations, he claimed, would bring down living costs, revive America’s industrial heartland and restore middle-class prosperity.

Has the president delivered? On October 22nd the White House claimed his economic policies were driving up wages and fuelling a “blue-collar BOOM”. America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained.

The most politically toxic policies are those that have raised daily costs. The president’s sweeping tariffs have pushed up the cost of consumer goods by roughly 2%, according to the New York Fed. The Budget Lab at Yale estimates they will cost the average household $1,100 this year. The war in Iran has also sent oil prices soaring, and is set to add another $1,000 to the average household’s costs by year’s end.

Pushing in the other direction, Mr Trump’s flagship tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has boosted tax refunds by around $340 on average. The law also created “Trump accounts”, an effort to broaden ownership in the stock market, with eligible newborns entitled to $1,000 to invest in shares. But the biggest gains went to richer Americans through lower taxes, even as the act tightened access to food stamps—with more than 5m Americans losing benefits so far—and to Medicaid, the government health-care programme for the poor.

To tally the net effects of these gains and losses, The Economist combined estimates of the impact of tariffs, higher petrol prices and Mr Trump’s tax-and-spending law across income groups in 2026. We estimate that Mr Trump’s policies will cost the poorest tenth of American households, with average income after taxes and transfers of around $37,000, almost 3% of their income. The richest tenth, with average after-tax incomes of nearly $500,000, will gain nearly 3% (see chart 1). Households in the middle, with average income of roughly $100,000, lose more than $400. That does not account for the effect of a decision, taken by congressional Republicans last year and endorsed by Mr Trump, to let enhanced Obamacare subsidies expire. That has raised average premiums for individual insurance purchased on exchanges by nearly $800 a year, according to KFF, a health-policy research group.

Housing costs pose another problem for the president. Mortgage rates, pushed up in part by the inflationary effects of his war in Iran, have climbed above 7%, prompting existing owners to stay put. Adding new supply has become more costly. Last year builders estimated that tariffs on materials would add nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new home. His immigration crackdown is fuelling labour shortages, too; in September a survey from the National Association of Home Builders reported that labour costs were up by 4.2% from a year earlier. It is lower-income and middle-class voters, again, who are most pinched. In May sales of starter homes fell by 5.4% from a year earlier, even as luxury-home sales rose by 6.2%, according to Zillow, an online property firm.

When it comes to jobs, health care and social assistance have accounted for almost all private-sector gains since January 2025, to meet demand from America’s ageing population. The AI boom has been another bright spot, with data-centre investment creating roughly 180,000 new jobs in industries related to the build-out. In other sectors, though, private employment has barely budged. Annual wage growth across the private sector has slowed from 4% to 3%; rising inflation means that workers’ hourly pay is 0.7% lower in real terms than a year ago. Labour’s share of non-farm business output has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1947 (changes to how business owners’ earnings are classified explain only some of the decline).

A renaissance in manufacturing jobs has been particularly elusive. Though manufacturing output has risen, manufacturing employment has fallen by some 20,000 since January 2025, while factory workers’ wages have failed to keep pace with inflation over the past year. In North Carolina, which Mr Trump won in 2024 and which now looks set to elect a Democrat to the Senate, nearly 9,000 factory jobs have disappeared over the past year.

Americans invested in the stock market have more to celebrate, as the AI bonanza has driven up the value of the S&P 500. But the impact is, once again, lopsided. Of the $17trn increase in Americans’ equity and mutual-fund wealth since the end of 2024, nearly 90% accrued to the richest tenth of households, compared with just 0.6% for the poorer half, according to data from the Federal Reserve (see chart 2).

These phenomena have not gone unnoticed. Nearly two-thirds of Americans think that Mr Trump’s economic policies have made conditions worse, according to a recent survey by the Pew Research Centre; the same is true of 35% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, nearly twice the share in January. Voters who are particularly affected by rising fuel costs and tariffs, such as farmers, are tilting towards Democrats. Mr Trump is now promising $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans retain control of Congress on November 3rd. That will do little to reassure voters who still feel left behind. ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

item.title: Democrats are rediscovering what an appealing politics of progress looks like
item.description:
United States

United States | Lexington Oct 29th 2026 Ever since Senator Tom Harkin retired after five terms in 2015, his fellow Democrats in Iowa have fared poorly. Republicans took control of what had been a divided state government and a divided congressional delegation, and Donald Trump won Iowa three tim...
item.content:encoded:
Democrats are rediscovering what an appealing politics of progress looks like

United States | Lexington

Oct 29th 2026

Ever since Senator Tom Harkin retired after five terms in 2015, his fellow Democrats in Iowa have fared poorly. Republicans took control of what had been a divided state government and a divided congressional delegation, and Donald Trump won Iowa three times, most recently by more than 13 points. Now a bit hard of hearing and frail at 86, Mr Harkin is back on the stump, to support Democratic candidates who are mounting surprisingly strong challenges up and down the ticket.

As elsewhere, a lot of the campaigning in Iowa has been stupid and awful. Record sums are being spent to jam the airways with advertisements making nasty, misleading claims. Mr Harkin’s presence is something of a tonic, and not only because he is as genial and plain-spoken as ever. When he introduces Josh Turek, who is campaigning for Mr Harkin’s old Senate seat, and Mr Turek pushes himself forward in his wheelchair to take the microphone, the exchange supplies a poignant reminder of the sort of thing all this politicking is supposed to be about.

Mr Harkin was the champion of the landmark civil-rights law banning discrimination against people with disabilities. Mr Turek, who was born with spina bifida, was 11 when that law, the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), passed in 1990. He calls Mr Harkin his political hero and says without the law, “every economic, every occupational, educational opportunity that I’ve been given would not have been there.” Like Mr Harkin himself, Mr Turek is quick to note something more. Mr Harkin counted on Republican allies to pass the bill. “It’s an amazing example of what we can do when we’re willing to work together,” Mr Turek says.

And that observation illuminates something else: that the struggle under way within the Democratic Party, which will probably grow more heated after the midterm elections, is not just a fight over policy between “progressives” and “moderates”. It is a contest between competing theories of how to make progress.

Mr Harkin is not surrendering the progressive label. He sees many of his differences with “my good friend” Bernie Sanders, the fiery leftist leader, as matters of style, even word-choice, not principle. He praises Mr Turek not only for having “a progressive agenda” but also for knowing “how to move it forward”. Mr Harkin does not note that Senator Sanders cannot point to any legislative achievement on the scale of the ADA.

Since Mr Harkin left the Senate, “progressive” has acquired a sharper edge. Mr Turek calls himself a moderate. Yet, like Mr Harkin, he also identifies as a prairie populist, in the tradition of the radical agrarian movement that united small farmers and trade unionists against the monopolistic powers of the Gilded Age. When Mr Turek talks about taxing billionaires, challenging big corporations and raising the minimum wage, he sounds no different from Abdul El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan and is the most prominent Senate candidate of the party’s populist left.

The candidates in Michigan and Iowa have important policy differences, though even those can blur. While Mr Turek says he opposes biological males competing in female sports, Dr El-Sayed has not taken a position, saying such decisions should be left to sports leagues. Unlike Mr Turek, Dr El-Sayed wants to abolish the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, yet he also says he supports applying immigration laws and securing the borders. Dr El-Sayed wants Medicare for All but says he would also back incremental expansions of public-health coverage favoured by Mr Turek. Dr El-Sayed wants to end military aid to Israel; Mr Turek would impose strict restrictions on such aid.

But their differences of style are stark. Dr El-Sayed has a combative, impatient approach, including to Democrats. He told donors he could intimidate Democrats who differ with him by putting “one ogre on a pike”, a reference to Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania. Mr Turek recoils from fighting even with Republicans. Dr El-Sayed has said Mr Trump should be impeached. Mr Turek has “no interest” in that. “We gotta get back to country over party,” he has said. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Mr Sanders’s likeliest heir, recently said a win by Dr El-Sayed would prove “anybody can win anywhere”. That is not so. Like Mr Turek, Dr El-Sayed is in a close race and may lose. But Michigan, where Democrats hold the governor’s office and both Senate seats, should have been less of a challenge.

The more inclusive style, rather than the combative one, has helped make Democrats competitive again this year not just in Iowa but in Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Texas. That model is the one Democrats should heed as they turn to the 2028 presidential campaign. Americans have been moving from Democrat-dominated states such as New York and California to Republican states including Florida and Texas. Congressional seats and electoral votes will follow along after the census in 2030. Expanding their electoral map is becoming an existential matter for Democrats. This may seem a paradox, and it will certainly be no easy feat in the last two years of Mr Trump’s polarising presidency, but to be viable as a party, Democrats need to become less partisan.

Republicans who are running scared this year are learning their version of that lesson. Mr Turek’s opponent, Representative Ashley Hinson, is calling herself a “bipartisan fighter for Iowa”. She barely mentioned Mr Trump at a rally in Manchester on October 25th. Americans, she said, were “feeling priced out of the American dream” because “a lot of people on, frankly, both sides of the aisle” have “forgotten how hard Iowans work”. The health-iest outcome of this refreshingly competitive election season across America would be a bipartisan awakening to the obvious: that most voters want less partisanship, more progress. ■

item.title: Lula, the great survivor, makes history

item.content:encoded:
Lula, the great survivor, makes history

The Americas | Brazil’s four-time winner

Oct 29th 2026

EVEN BY BRAZIL’S standards, it was a week of extraordinary drama. On October 25th Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who most pundits thought was dead and buried after the first round of voting, won Brazil’s presidential election. That stunning comeback vaults Lula, as the 81-year-old left-winger is known, into an exclusive club of presidents who have won four democratic elections. Two days later his defeated rival, Flávio Bolsonaro—the son of Jair, a hard-right former president who is under house arrest for attempting a coup—fled Brazil after a Supreme Court judge investigating allegations of corruption ordered him to hand in his passports. He has taken his family to the United States.

No presidential candidate since the return of democracy in 1985 had lost the first round of voting and won the run-off. Lula trailed Flávio by 2m votes in the first ballot on October 4th. The candidates who were knocked out at that stage, who between them had received 8% of votes, also chose to back Flávio. Yet in less than three weeks Lula gained an extra 10m votes, many of them from people who had failed to turn out or spoiled their ballots in the first round (see chart 1).

Three things explain the turnaround. The first is a change in tactics. Ahead of the first round, Lula ran a disorganised and old-fashioned campaign. He wore a Panama hat to hide scars from a recent operation; that merely reminded voters of his age. His team barely spent anything on social media. Instead they handed out lots of stickers with his face on them. But between the two rounds Lula discovered both his mojo and the internet. He lost the hat and he began posting selfie videos on Instagram. His campaign got a huge boost from André Janones, a congressman from Minas Gerais, a bellwether state, who set up a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” which attracted over 10m members in two weeks. Mr Janones gave the members of this group “missions”, such as reposting an image of Lula on social media, which helped his messages go viral in the final stretch of the campaign.

Second, the government opened the taps. Lula raised handouts in Brazil’s flagship welfare programme by 15%. He pushed Congress into passing a law to reduce the working week by a day, without pay cuts. He pledged to make public transport free at weekends and forgive federal debts for sole traders, as well as to hand out $1,000 to a million of them. Incumbents in Brazil often make lavish giveaways before elections, but even so Lula has been generous. His team has not explained how he will fund these and other freebies, which are expected to cost 2% of GDP by the end of next year.

Finally, many Brazilians decided that Flávio was beyond the pale. Two televised debates helped rehash his dodgy past, especially his alleged links to Rio de Janeiro’s militias—groups of corrupt policemen who work as hitmen and extortionists. (Two weeks after the first-round vote, one of Flávio’s allies in Rio was arrested on charges of working with militiamen and drug-traffickers.)

The debates may have been decisive. In one of them Flávio, who is a lawyer, was asked about a case in which he defended a policeman accused of killing a five-year-old girl, which many viewers had not heard about. His arrogance turned voters off, not least when he mocked Lula for having nine fingers. (Lula lost one finger while working in a factory as a teenager.) “I was a minor and working at night, because either I worked or I did not eat,” Lula replied. That highlighted Flávio’s better-off background, and that he got his start in politics thanks to his father.

When his defeat was announced on October 25th, Flávio seemed defiant. He refused to concede (even though he had lost by a reasonable margin, having chalked up 48% of votes compared with 52% for Lula). He argued unconvincingly that a last-minute Supreme Court decision to keep polling stations open for an additional two hours, because of extreme weather and disruptions to public transport, had disadvantaged his campaign. He called for the vote to be annulled.

Yet then events moved very fast. Having failed in his tilt at the presidency, Flávio will in February lose the judicial immunity he has enjoyed as a sitting senator. Recently federal police have been investigating his ties to a businessman accused of massive money-laundering (both he and the businessman deny wrongdoing). The day after the election, the Supreme Court judge who is handling that case banned him from leaving the country.

Police say Flávio did not comply with a request to surrender his passports. Instead, on the evening of October 27th he and his family crossed the border into Argentina. The group then travelled to Miami via Ecuador (the US State Department had said in advance that the United States would be willing to grant them entry). Flávio’s brother, Eduardo, has himself been living in the United States since 2025. In June a Brazilian court sentenced Eduardo in absentia to four years in jail for trying to unduly influence the prosecution of his father—by lobbying Donald Trump to apply sanctions on the judges who sentenced him.

After arriving in the United States Flávio published a statement in which he called himself “the leader of Brazil”, said he was the victim of a “witch hunt”, and vowed to keep leading the opposition from abroad. For the moment Mr Trump does not seem much inclined to back him, beyond permitting him to stay in the country. On October 26th Mr Trump told reporters that Brazil’s vote “looked like another rigged election” while adding that he “didn’t take sides” and saying “I like Lula, I get along with him very well.” On October 28th he said, “I won’t get involved”.

In theory, Flávio’s departure could prove a chance for Brazil’s right to make a fresh start. He became the right’s candidate only because his father anointed him as his heir. That decision sidelined politicians who would have been much more electable. With Jair under house arrest and Flávio abroad, there could now be an opportunity for renewal.

All this has got Lula’s new mandate off to a dramatic start. His honeymoon is going to be short. Though he has won the presidency, right-wingers constitute the largest caucus in both houses. That will make it difficult for Lula to govern, especially since constitutional limits (and his age) mean that he cannot run again. He could become a lame duck from day one.

Brazil’s creaking economy must be his number-one priority. Thanks to his own spendthrift policies, the central bank has pushed up real interest rates to vertigo-inducing heights. Government debt-to-GDP has risen by over ten percentage points during Lula’s current four-year term. Markets panicked when his surprise victory was announced (see chart 2): the real fell by 8% against the dollar—its worst day in more than a quarter of a century—and São Paulo’s stock index closed down 14%. Investors are demanding that Lula appoint a heavyweight as finance minister, rather than a party cadre, and that he set out a credible plan for lower spending. It is worrying that his pre-election giveaways suggest he will not choose to do anything of the sort.

Lula beat the odds to win the presidency. But he will need a lot more luck—and much good judgment—if he is to make a success of his fourth and final term. ■

Sign up to El Boletín, our subscriber-only newsletter on Latin America, to understand the forces shaping a fascinating and complex region.

item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普的任性是西班牙的机遇

美洲 | 欧洲对冲 2026年10月29日

让拉丁美洲领导人共处一室已属不易，让他们在任何问题上达成一致更是难上加难。两年前在厄瓜多尔举行的伊比利亚-美洲峰会（西班牙、葡萄牙和拉丁美洲领导人两年一度的聚会）上，该地区只有一位总统出席——而且那位总统还是东道主。人们寄希望于西班牙今年能做得更好，这次峰会将于11月4日至5日在马德里举行。组织者力争让多达18位国家元首或其副手出席。时机十分有利。唐纳德·特朗普越来越把拉丁美洲视为美国的后院。尽管一波表面上与特朗普结盟的总统已经上台，但该地区仍然希望通过贸易多元化来对冲他的不可预测性。与中国的关系很重要，但也问题重重。“我从未见过对欧洲如此强烈的渴望，”一位资深拉丁美洲外交官表示。西班牙与该地区的联系是世界两个超级大国都无法复制的。超过400万出生在拉丁美洲的人现在生活在西班牙，其中许多人是在过去十年中抵达的。早在20世纪80年代和90年代，西班牙的民主转型曾是其中一些前殖民地的榜样。1982年至1996年担任首相的费利佩·冈萨雷斯成为该地区多国政府的顾问。1991年，西班牙和墨西哥在瓜达拉哈拉召集了首届伊比利亚-美洲峰会，为一个由22个成员组成的共同体奠定了基础，这一共同体松散地效仿了前英国殖民地组成的英联邦。自那以后，西班牙的影响力逐渐减弱。西班牙企业仍是该地区的重要投资者。但在拉丁美洲与中国加强关系的同时，它们却有所退缩。一些外交官抱怨说，西班牙政府对此越来越不感兴趣。现任首相佩德罗·桑切斯——他已宣布于11月29日举行大选——希望改善这种状况。这需要改变做法。桑切斯与左翼政府相处得最好，与右翼领导人的关系则一直很紧张。2024年，在阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱的一次演讲中侮辱桑切斯夫人之后，西班牙暂时撤回了驻布宜诺斯艾利斯的大使。西班牙尚未接受哥伦比亚新总统派往马德里的大使。议员们抱怨说，这位特使在社交媒体上说了桑切斯的坏话。然而，即使拥有共同的世界观也不一定能保证良好的关系。从纸面上看，桑切斯和墨西哥左翼总统克劳迪娅·欣鲍姆应该像吉事果配巧克力一样合拍。但欣鲍姆的前任兼导师安德烈斯·曼努埃尔·洛佩斯·奥夫拉多尔曾就西班牙的殖民历史挑起争端，并要求西班牙国王为征服道歉。西班牙外交部作出防御性反应；当墨西哥在2024年没有邀请西班牙国王出席欣鲍姆的就职典礼时，争端进一步恶化。事实证明，欣鲍姆更愿意将历史积怨与当下利益分开。咨询公司Signum Global Advisors的拉斐尔·查指出，她有充分的理由这样做。美国是墨西哥最大的贸易伙伴，但特朗普反复无常的政策制定正在使两国关系松动。在经济增长乏力的情况下，欣鲍姆任由与西班牙的外交争端拖延下去毫无益处。委内瑞拉临时总统德尔西·罗德里格斯很可能会出席马德里会议。罗德里格斯是在特朗普的支持下执政的，因此拉丁美洲人不太可能对她出席大惊小怪。但在西班牙，这将引发争议。反对派长期以来一直指责西班牙左翼纵容委内瑞拉严酷的政权。如果峰会大声呼吁加快该国的民主转型，那将令人耳目一新——也有利于西班牙的形象。聚集在马德里的人将讨论人工智能、防灾准备以及学位等教育资格的互认问题。这类话题可能显得低调。但其他区域组织，如拉美和加勒比国家共同体和美洲国家组织，正处于低谷。因此，也许最重要的是大家能聚在一起。■

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Back in Venezuela, María Corina Machado may speed the return of democracy

The Americas | Homecoming queen

Oct 29th 2026

It was, as is her style, a homecoming laden with symbolism. On October 25th the first images to be released of María Corina Machado’s return to Venezuela showed the opposition leader surrounded by supporters next to the statue of the Divina Pastora. The shrine, in a church near the city of Barquisimeto, depicts the Virgin Mary as a shepherdess guiding her flock.

Her return after a ten-month exile took millions of Venezuelans—and possibly the country’s ruling regime—by surprise. For months the wildly popular politician (pictured) had been promising to come back “soon” to Venezuela. She had been there (albeit in hiding) until December, when she left the country to collect the Nobel peace prize. In recent months she had made several attempts to get back. On each occasion it seemed the regime foiled her plans. This time she crossed the land border from Colombia.

Her presence in Venezuela will complicate the unusual, cosy relationship the administration of Donald Trump has formed with the disreputable regime of Delcy Rodríguez. Ms Rodríguez, who has quietly dropped the “interim” from her presidential title in recent weeks, has been running the country since January 3rd, when special forces captured her then boss, Nicolás Maduro, and took him to face drug-trafficking charges in New York.

Mr Trump claimed not to know about Ms Machado’s return when he was asked about it. “She is a very nice woman,” he said on October 25th. “She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?” In January Ms Machado handed the medal, which she won for her campaign for democracy in Venezuela, to Mr Trump (who claimed to deserve it more). She said at the time she made the gesture in gratitude for his “decisive support of our cause”.

She has plenty of reason to doubt the extent of that support. Mr Trump’s praise for Ms Rodríguez—whom he calls “terrific”—has always been fulsome. But he has long been ambivalent towards Ms Machado, a former congresswoman from a once wealthy industrialist family who was persecuted by Mr Maduro. She has called for new elections in Venezuela, to be held by next July, and says she will stand as a candidate. This has not got Mr Trump’s backing. “I don’t think they’re ready [for elections] yet,” he said in September.

His focus instead has been on portraying the capture of Mr Maduro and its aftermath as an unmitigated success. His government in August secured majority control of 65bn barrels of the country’s oil, about a fifth of its proven reserves, in an agreement with Venezuela and a private oil company. “We took over Venezuela very successfully and they’ve sent me as a gift a boatload of a million barrels of oil,” he bragged at a campaign event in Texas, on October 27th. He later quipped that maybe Venezuela “will become a prosperous 51st state”. He often claims that Venezuelans are “dancing in the streets” in celebration of all he has achieved.

Mr Trump’s problem, and Ms Machado’s opportunity, is that none of this is true. Few Venezuelans view his propping up of Ms Rodríguez, or their own economic situation, as a success story. Mr Trump’s own popularity in Venezuela has slumped in recent months. “He got rid of Maduro, which is good, but it is basically the same shit here,” says Eduardo, a computer technician in Caracas, the capital.

America insists that it has a plan with Venezuela, and that it is on track. On October 26th an official at the State Department said the next stage of the “transition” is to replace the members of Venezuela’s Supreme Court by mid-December, followed by an overhaul of the electoral council. The idea is that Ms Rodríguez would then at some point declare the presidency “vacant”, triggering elections within six months. Perhaps that would be in late 2027, or 2028. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said after Ms Machado’s return that the Rodríguez regime would not be allowed to wait out the process until the Trump administration ends: “We have timelines that are agreed to, and so far, they’ve met every one.”

Will Ms Machado abide by the same timeline? Or will she try to accelerate it? On October 25th a caravan of supporters accompanied her in a triumphant return to Caracas. For a giddy few hours, Venezuelans really were dancing in the streets. And it was not to Mr Trump’s tune. ■

item.content:encoded:
本雅明·内塔尼亚胡没有赢，但也没有输

中东与非洲 | 有得有失 2026年10月29日

本雅明·内塔尼亚胡在10月28日凌晨走上讲台时，已经知道自己几乎肯定失去了议会多数席位。然而，内塔尼亚胡先生和他的利库德党支持者们却欢欣鼓舞。利库德集团失去了一些席位，但它仍然是以色列最大的政党。选民惩罚了执政联盟，因为大多数以色列人认为内塔尼亚胡先生的失误导致了2023年10月7日的大屠杀，也因为他的联盟奉行的分裂政策。但这次打击远没有大多数民调机构预测的那么严重。更重要的是，利库德支持者认为，尽管反对派赢得了绝对多数，但它无法组建一个替代他们的联盟。他们很可能是对的。

随着超过90%的选票被统计，内塔尼亚胡先生的联盟在以色列议会（克内塞特）的120个席位中赢得了53席。最终结果在本期《经济学人》付印时仍在统计中，预计不会有太大变化：总理将没有足够的席位来组建新政府。

以色列反对派分为两个阵营。主要阵营由四个以犹太人为主的政党组成，预计将赢得48席。第二个阵营以阿拉伯政党为主，有望赢得19席，这是以色列阿拉伯少数群体有史以来赢得的最多席位。两个阵营合计可以掌控明确的多数。

但在四个犹太反对党中，只有一个——左倾的民主党——明确表示愿意与阿拉伯政党共同组建政府。另外两个较大的反对党则更加犹豫。由前以色列国防军参谋长加迪·艾森科特领导的亚沙尔党，以及由两位前总理纳夫塔利·贝内特和亚伊尔·拉皮德领导的雅赫德党（团结党）一直含糊其辞。反对党民族团结党（以色列贝泰努）领导人阿维格多尔·利伯曼是民族主义者，他明确排除甚至在非正式基础上依赖阿拉伯政党的可能性。

就阿拉伯政党而言，他们愿意合作。在曼苏尔·阿巴斯的领导下，温和的伊斯兰组织拉姆自2018年以来一直渴望成为政府的一部分。阿巴斯先生认为这是促进以色列阿拉伯人利益的最佳方式。联合名单是一个由阿拉伯、共产主义和巴勒斯坦民族主义政党组成的更大选举联盟，则更为谨慎。加入联盟意味着要共同承担政策责任，例如安全政策——这是它所反对的。但在10月10日，联合名单领导人优素福·贾巴林表示，该组织将利用其掌握的所有“工具”来取代内塔尼亚胡政府，并将成为新联盟的“安全网”，即使它不会成为正式成员。

选举前，艾森科特先生和其他犹太反对派领导人在私下承认，他们需要阿拉伯政党的席位。他们宣扬组建少数派政府的想法，该政府将依赖与阿拉伯政党达成的信任与供给协议。但他们没有公开表态。内塔尼亚胡先生在竞选中一直指责对手计划把阿拉伯人拉入政府。在一个AI生成的视频中，艾森科特先生被描绘成骑在一匹木制特洛伊马上，而阿巴斯先生和民主党领导人亚伊尔·戈兰则潜伏其中。戈兰先生指出，与以色列阿拉伯人进行政治合作并无不妥。艾森科特先生和其他政党领导人则回避了这个问题。

在1992年的选举中，阿拉伯政党支持工党领袖伊扎克·拉宾，阻挡了利库德集团的执政之路。他们并未正式加入拉宾先生的政府，但在关键投票中给予支持，作为回报获得了对其社区增加的拨款。时任利库德集团领导人伊扎克·沙米尔毫无异议地接受了失败。但他的继任者内塔尼亚胡先生将贬低阿拉伯人选票作为其核心政治目标之一。在1996年他作为利库德领导人的首次选举中，内塔尼亚胡先生打出了“内塔尼亚胡：对犹太人有益”的口号。2015年，他在选举日发布了一段视频，警告支持者“阿拉伯选民正成群结队地前往投票站”，并敦促他们也这样做。他指责对手计划与“支持恐怖主义”和“穆斯林兄弟会”的阿拉伯议员同坐政府之中，这种指控在他的竞选中屡见不鲜，尽管在2021年组建联盟失败后，他本人曾与阿巴斯先生讨论过加入联盟的事宜。他的极右翼盟友扼杀了这些会谈。阿巴斯先生转而加入了由贝内特先生和拉皮德先生领导的短暂（前一届）联盟。

这一次内塔尼亚胡先生又如法炮制。“右翼集团在犹太复国主义公众、犹太公众中拥有压倒性多数，”他在选举日说。“绝对不能冒险让以色列组建一个依赖反犹太复国主义、反对我们生存的阿拉伯政党的政府。”自10月7日袭击事件以来，他和他的联盟在民调中一直萎靡不振。当他们终于走向全国大选时，普遍预计他们会遭到惨败并被赶下台。联盟没有被彻底击溃，部分原因是内塔尼亚胡先生煽动了反巴勒斯坦的恐惧。这可能没有提升他自己的声望，但确实帮助减少了对对手的支持。

“我憎恶内塔尼亚胡和他的联盟，”特拉维夫的软件工程师什穆埃尔·戴维森说。“但我不能投票给一个可能与想杀了我的阿拉伯政党合作的反对派。”大多数阿拉伯政客谴责了10月7日的袭击，但有些人却麻木不仁。拉姆党的一位议员将哈马斯描述为“部分是一个慈善组织”。联合名单中巴勒斯坦民族主义政党巴拉德的领导人萨米·阿布·谢哈德称这次屠杀是“一个具有军事、政治和战略意义的重要历史事件”，其他人可以从中学习。这样的言论帮助内塔尼亚胡先生煽动以色列犹太人的恐惧，让他们认为他们的阿拉伯邻居——其中大多数人认同自己是巴勒斯坦人——在以色列-巴勒斯坦冲突中站在对立面。

由于迫切希望现任执政联盟下台，阿拉伯人在10月27日以数十年来最高的投票率前往投票站。他们的政党领导人一直在向犹太对手伸出橄榄枝。“阿拉伯代表权应该带来影响力和伙伴关系，”阿巴斯先生在选举夜说。“我们准备好并愿意为推翻内塔尼亚胡政府铺平道路，”贾巴林先生第二天在社交媒体上发帖说。“变革来自犹太-阿拉伯伙伴关系。”他们的犹太对手尚未回应。在选举夜的演讲中，艾森科特、贝内特和拉皮德先生都谈到要组建“犹太复国主义政府”，但没有提及阿拉伯政党及其令人瞩目的收获。此后，他们一直保持沉默。

一位反对派议员建议，当新一届立法机构于11月10日宣誓就职时，犹太和阿拉伯反对党可以在选举新议长方面进行合作，并控制议会事务。如果这样的举动成功，也许可以促成联盟谈判。但一位反对派领导人的高级助手给这种想法浇了冷水，称更有可能的是其中一些政党会寻求与内塔尼亚胡先生组建团结政府，而不是与阿拉伯人合作。到目前为止，在犹太反对派阵营中，只有戈兰先生提出了不同的路线。“我们不能再接受内塔尼亚胡对犹太选票和阿拉伯选票的种族主义划分，”他在选举次日说，并呼吁“组建一个为所有以色列公民服务的政府”。

但内塔尼亚胡先生似乎有信心，他可以在反对派犯错时静待时机。即使没有多数席位，他也会继续担任看守总理；他似乎仍然希望，在美国中期选举之后，唐纳德·特朗普可能会同意与他一起对伊朗发动进一步的军事打击。以色列有一个独特的机会，他在选举夜宣称，“与我们的伙伴特朗普总统一起，一劳永逸地消除伊朗的威胁”。如果特朗普先生决定加入另一次袭击，或者让以色列发动一次袭击，内塔尼亚胡先生确信他的一些对手会加入由他领导的团结政府，或者他将能够拖延联盟谈判，并押注于2027年初的又一次选举。■

item.title: 沙特阿拉伯希望伊朗叫停胡塞武装并与美国达成协议
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
沙特阿拉伯希望伊朗叫停胡塞武装并与美国达成协议

中东与非洲 | 一趟尴尬的差事 2026年10月29日 数月来，伊朗的盟友用导弹和无人机猛烈攻击沙特阿拉伯。它们破坏了沙特最重要的输油管道，并在利雅得机场造成至少17人死亡，该机场至今大部分时间仍处于停运状态。因此，当沙特国防大臣哈立德·本·萨勒曼于10月26日飞往德黑兰进行旨在“鼓励对话”的访问时，着实令不少人感到意外。这位沙特王储的兄弟满面笑容，甚至与伊朗最高安全官员穆赫辛·雷扎伊合影留念。这次会面出人意料，就连沙特官方媒体似乎都未曾预料。双方都急于对此进行解读。伊朗官员将其视为自身实力的展示：一位沙特高级王室成员像请愿者一样到来。一名强硬派议员称，这个“无助”的王国不得不“乞求”与胡塞武装进行调解——胡塞武装是也门受伊朗支持的民兵组织，大部分破坏行动都是他们所为。不过，哈立德王子并非独自前往。与他一同出现在德黑兰的还有巴基斯坦陆军参谋长和土耳其情报机构负责人。这两个国家都是“麦加协议”的成员——该共同防御协议于8月在沙特阿拉伯签署。沙特方面将这次峰会定性为一种威慑展示，即三大穆斯林大国共同向孤立无援的伊朗发出警告。尽管场面颇具戏剧性，但这次峰会似乎收效甚微。沙特提出了两个迫在眉睫的关切。其一是胡塞武装。然而，伊朗几乎没有动机去约束他们。事实上，在哈立德王子访问之后，利雅得又遭遇了更多导弹袭击。其二是美国与伊朗之间再度开战的风险。唐纳德·特朗普已警告海湾国家，他准备在下周中期选举后发起又一轮打击。美国正向该地区派遣军舰、防空炮组及其他装备。第三艘航空母舰预计将于11月抵达。世界大部分地区都在拼命试图阻止这一切。卡塔尔和巴基斯坦的代表团——它们曾通过谈判达成此前的停战协议——本月已多次访问德黑兰。欧洲外交官们正忙于电话斡旋。甚至弗拉基米尔·普京似乎也在插手此事。他本周在莫斯科与伊朗总统和卡塔尔埃米尔举行了会谈。然而，这一连串外交活动并未产生伊朗和美国都能接受的协议。伊朗坚持要达成一项以霍尔木兹海峡为核心的窄范围协议。如果美国解除对伊朗港口的封锁、取消制裁并做出其他经济让步，伊朗政权承诺将在一周内重新开放该航道。海湾外交官们正在就时间表讨价还价：也许伊朗会同意四天，而不是七天。但这忽略了一个更大的问题。特朗普先生对这样的协议不感兴趣，因为它在本质上相当于回到他在6月签署的那份短命的谅解备忘录。总统希望伊朗在核计划上立即做出让步。迄今为止，伊朗并不愿意；在德黑兰的四边会谈中，它甚至拒绝讨论核问题。该地区的外交官表示，沙特向伊朗提供了胡萝卜加大棒。如果伊朗做出让步，从而能够与美国达成协议，沙特及其邻国愿意讨论更广泛的地区安全 pact。如果伊朗拒绝并恢复对海湾国家的攻击，麦加协议成员国将做好回应的准备。风险在于，伊朗认为这两者都不可信。伊朗怀疑沙特是否认同其对地区安全的看法——其中包括将美军赶出海湾。至于大棒，沙特已经在艰难地抵御胡塞武装，而其新盟友也不愿参与进攻性打击。在依赖美国数十年之后，海湾国家如今正试图自行化解地区危机。这是一种值得欢迎的努力——但就目前而言，战争的威胁仍然挥之不去。■

item.title: South Africa’s “white party” looks for more black votes
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Gogo a-go-go Oct 29th 2026 AS PART OF her campaign to become mayor of Johannesburg, Helen Zille has snorkelled in a water-filled pothole. She has directed cars when power cuts turned off traffic lights. She has paddled down a flooded street. The candidate from the Demo...
item.content:encoded:
South Africa’s “white party” looks for more black votes

Middle East & Africa | Gogo a-go-go

Oct 29th 2026

AS PART OF her campaign to become mayor of Johannesburg, Helen Zille has snorkelled in a water-filled pothole. She has directed cars when power cuts turned off traffic lights. She has paddled down a flooded street. The candidate from the Democratic Alliance (DA), South Africa’s second-biggest party, has taken an old BMW “spinning”, a popular pursuit in the city’s black townships. The 75-year-old grandmother has stepped up to a turntable (pictured) and been dubbed “DJ Gogo”.

These were stunts with a purpose. Ahead of local elections on November 4th Ms Zille wants to highlight the decay of the commercial capital under a coalition led by the African National Congress (ANC). Polls suggest the once hegemonic party will have its worst showing in a nationwide election since the end of white rule in 1994. Meanwhile Ms Zille could soon be the first white mayor of post-apartheid Johannesburg. Such a result would underline the decline of the party of Nelson Mandela—and perhaps point to the beginnings of a less racialised politics.

The ANC has been losing support for 20 years. But it is heading for a new low. An average of opinion polls in the past six months has the ANC at 32%, the DA at 27%. Five years ago the ANC won 46% to the DA’s 22%. The DA’s own polling reckons it could become the largest party in most of South Africa’s eight largest cities.

Among the roughly 80% of the South African population that is black, the ANC remains the most popular party. It benefits from residual loyalty because of its role in ending apartheid, its patronage and because it genuinely improved the country during its early years in office. But South Africans are increasingly tired of its graft and failure to run basic services. Johannesburg, which sells itself as a “world-class African city”, is the most glaring example. Nearly half of the bulk water the city supplies is never paid for because it is stolen or leaks out of pipes. It spends more money than it raises in taxes and fees, yet it consistently fails to repair infrastructure. The cost of fixing its infrastructure backlog is roughly 25 times its capital budget.

“This is our last chance to save Johannesburg,” argues Ms Zille. Based on her experience running Cape Town from 2006 to 2009, she pledges to get a grip on the finances, appoint leaders to city agencies on merit and root out corruption.

Whether she gets the chance will depend on her ability to form a coalition. The DA usually benefits from “differential turnout”: its core base among whites and other minorities is more likely to vote than black voters are. But since black Joburgers make up around three-quarters of the city, she will need enough of their votes, too.

Will she get them? Most former ANC supporters either do not vote or opt for an opposition party other than the DA. UmKhonto we Sizwe (MK), led by Jacob Zuma, a former president, targets Zulus, the largest ethnic group. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) is another black-nationalist party. Other urban voters are attracted by ActionSA, whose appeal is based partly on its ability to exploit concerns about illegal immigration. “A country without order is headed for disaster,” says Sanele Bhagathi, a voter from Johannesburg.

Many black South Africans are DA-curious but have resisted it because, fairly or unfairly, the DA’s brand is that of a “white party”. Sceptics see Cape Town, which is well run but has bleak mostly non-white outskirts, as a reason for caution. “I don’t believe the party cares enough about [that inequality], and they should,” says Thabo Nthuli, another voter in Johannesburg.

Yet governing in coalition with the ANC at a national level has helped detoxify the DA’s image and reaffirmed its reputation for competence. It is hard for opponents to suggest that the likes of Ms Zille want to bring back apartheid—a trope of the ANC—when as a journalist under white rule she exposed the regime’s abuses.

For many black voters Cape Town is a model of good governance. “I never used to have these problems or these failures,” says Mandisa Maphisa, who moved to Johannesburg from there. “I’ll be voting for the DA for effective service delivery that the party itself has proven is possible.”

The DA thinks it will double its share of the black vote, from around 4.5% to 9% nationally, meaning it could be the third-most popular party among black South Africans. Ms Zille will probably win a higher share, though she may not meet her target of 40% of the overall vote.

The shift away from the ANC suggests that politics is beginning to catch up with society. Most South Africans say they do not mind the race of their neighbour, their sons- or daughters-in-law or the president. In a survey published in April, 70% agreed that politicians use race and colonialism as an excuse for their own failures.

An increasingly diverse middle class shapes politics, too. In 2012 black households made up 29% of those with at least 75,000 rand ($4,500) in monthly income, notes the Liberty Institute, a research group at the University of Cape Town. By 2024 they had caught up with whites (41%). The share of multiracial marriages increased from 1% to 11% between 2001 and 2022. More South Africans socialise with people of other races than in the 2000s.

There is no guarantee that Ms Zille will end up as mayor. But if she can win over enough black voters to form a coalition in Johannesburg, that will draw “a line in the sand”, says William Gumede, an academic. “To get the South Africa we want, we need more blacks to cross the racial barrier.” ■

Sign up to the Analysing Africa, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

item.content:encoded:
塞内加尔尝试用第一语言教育更多儿童

中东与非洲 | 走向本土化 2026年10月29日

当塞内加尔政府想弄清楚应该用哪种语言教育儿童时，它派遣官员进入学校，听孩子们玩耍时的对话。在全国各地的学校操场上，调查人员发现孩子们用沃洛夫语和普拉尔语交谈，用萨菲语开玩笑，偶尔夹杂一个法语单词。这项摸底工作是2021年启动的一项推广塞内加尔本土语言教学计划的一部分。塞内加尔大多数学校使用法语授课，法语是该国唯一的官方语言。但大多数孩子并不能很好地理解或使用法语。塞内加尔希望通过先用本土语言教育幼童，再逐步过渡到其他语言，让孩子们学到更多知识。目前，许多上法语学校的孩子几乎听不懂课程内容。在首都达喀尔，估计有55%的儿童不会说法语。在该国南部的法蒂克等农村地区，这一比例上升到87%。

这一情况与非洲大陆其他地区相似。大多数非洲学校使用国际语言授课，但据认为只有10%到15%的非洲人能够流利使用其中一种。他们通常会说非洲1500至3000种本土语言中的几种。但由于大多数孩子没有接受过母语的正式教育，母语往往发展不足，无法成为学习学校所要求的新语言的基础。结果，许多人很难在任何语言上真正学好。澳大利亚圣母大学的研究人员恩兰拉·姆波富表示，在她研究的一个南非班级中，大约80%的九岁和十岁孩子能完美地读出一个句子，但并不理解句子的含义。

本土语言教学似乎有所帮助。2024年在南非进行的一项研究发现，专注于用母语学习阅读的孩子在国际语言方面也表现更好，而专注于国际语言的较弱学生用母语阅读的能力则较差。在塞内加尔，最近的这一努力似乎也提高了阅读分数。然而，此前由世界银行和美国国际开发署资助的本土语言教学项目在那里遭遇了挫折，部分原因是家长对教科书粗制滥造感到不满，与法语授课的教材相比差距明显。

考虑到非洲各地语言众多，一个重要的决定是选择哪种本土语言进行教学。例如，塞内加尔除官方语言法语外，还有六种宪法承认的语言，但总共有至少30种语言。佛罗里达大学的菲奥娜·麦克劳林表示，语言统计数据陈旧且不完整，偏爱某一种语言可能会在政治上带来棘手问题。她估计，沃洛夫语是大约40%塞内加尔人的第一语言，90%的人会说这种语言。但沃洛夫语的传播及其在达喀尔作为通用语言的地位，引发了“沃洛夫化”的担忧，尤其是在基督教信仰为主的南部地区，那里许多人将这种语言与伊斯兰教联系在一起。

为了缓解这些担忧，塞内加尔官员逐校决定推荐使用哪种语言。协助实施该项目的组织“教育与发展研究伙伴”的负责人马马杜·利表示，学校很灵活。例如，在普拉尔语占多数的地区，以索宁克语为主的村庄里的孩子将用索宁克语学习。有一个案例中，一所学校最初用沃洛夫语教学，但两年后一些家长希望孩子说普拉尔语。学校将班级分开，以便两种语言都能教授。

也许最大的挑战是让家长放心，本土语言教学不会挤掉英语、法语或葡萄牙语的教学。前殖民国家的语言仍然主导着法律、政治和商业，对成功至关重要。塞内加尔采用渐进式过渡。孩子们最初用所选的本土语言学习80%的时间，用法语学习20%的时间。到12岁时，这一比例颠倒过来。“孩子们应该扎根于自己的文化，但也应该向世界开放。”利先生说。■

订阅《分析非洲》周刊，了解全球最年轻、也最不被理解的大陆的最新动态。

item.title: 塞尔维亚学生找到推翻强人的新方法
item.description:
Europe

item.content:encoded:
塞尔维亚学生找到推翻强人的新方法

欧洲 | 众人登场 2026年10月29日。18个月来，贝尔格莱德市中心的前卫公园一直是政治热点。2025年初，抗议学生占领了该公园。随后，效忠塞尔维亚领导人亚历山大·武契奇的力量将其围起并设立了营地。10月25日，即塞尔维亚大选当天，一队黑衣男子聚集，他们似乎是亲政府的暴徒。但在武契奇意外宣布败选后，他们便消失了。次日，围栏被拆除，帐篷被摧毁，市民象征性地夺回了公园。夺回该国的其他机构将更加困难。武契奇及其塞尔维亚进步党（SNS）统治了14年，主导着法院、媒体和经济。他的败选规模出乎意料。民调显示，SNS与反对派“学生名单”——一个基本没有领导人的抗议运动——势均力敌。然而，SNS仅获得39%的选票。学生赢得了53%的选票，在250个席位的议会中获得141个席位。他们将试图为武契奇捕获的国家恢复法治。与4月被广泛民众运动击败的匈牙利总理欧尔班·维克托一样，武契奇因腐败引发的愤怒而下台。加入SNS已成为在国有关联机构和大型企业中职业晋升的必需条件，这种共产主义式做法导致了犬儒主义和不满。2021年，因反对拟议的锂矿开采，爆发了大规模示威。2024年，一座火车站雨棚坍塌造成16人死亡，被归咎于黑心承包商；塞尔维亚人开始感到政府腐败已使无人安全。这引发了学生运动，从大学开始，在全国各地举行大规模集会，然后以院系为基础的“全体会议”形式聚集，选举候选人参加大选。“学生名单”将如何执政异常不明朗。其议员均无政治背景；他们是按专业知识选出的公民社会成员。塞尔维亚人猜测权力将归于新部长，还是归于推选他们的学生。一位可能的总理人选是德扬·绍什基奇，曾任塞尔维亚国家银行行长，现为学生名单议员。他表示，一旦上任，政府“将与其他任何政府一样运作”。议员们已签署该运动的宣言，保证学生将拥有“非常重要的影响力”。然而，该宣言充满“负责任地使用公共资金”的承诺，却缺乏具体细节。学生旨在吸引每一位厌倦SNS的选民，不论其政治倾向如何。该运动包罗万象，从强硬民族主义者到随和的自由派。最后一场选举集会吸引了15万人，现场有戴头巾的波什尼亚克穆斯林、描绘耶稣的东正教旗帜，以及塞尔维亚网球冠军诺瓦克·德约科维奇的纸板立牌。长远来看，该运动可能分裂为左、中、右派系。在外交政策上，其纲领与武契奇的政策几乎没有区别。它反对科索沃独立，回避对俄罗斯的制裁。绍什基奇对塞尔维亚是否将继续向乌克兰出售武器态度含糊：学生们“不支持从灾难中获取经济利益的想法”。但如果塞尔维亚政府在法治方面取得进展，其加入欧盟的努力可能受益。武契奇已辞去总统职务（他无资格再次竞选总统），以便竞选总理。一些人曾担心他可能诉诸舞弊或暴力而非放弃权力。舞弊确实存在，但不足以影响结果。在武契奇下台后出任代理总统的SNS成员安娜·布尔纳比奇表示，随着计票结果出炉并明确毫无胜选之路时，“他说‘没有理由不宣布这一结果……我们输了，就这样。’”SNS主要是一部庇护机器，分发工作、公共合同和金钱。失去这一权力后，它可能无法在反对派中兴旺，甚至可能无法生存。清洗其官僚的努力已经开始。本周，学生名单的支持者愤怒地与一家亲武契奇报纸的老板对峙，并要求公共广播公司的编辑辞职，该广播公司此前拒绝报道学生抗议活动。布尔纳比奇称此类要求为“革命恐怖”。作为一名公开出柜的同性恋女性、部分克罗地亚血统的她表示，自大选以来她一直收到威胁信息，称她为“克罗地亚婊子”和“死同性恋”。然而，SNS仍拥有资源。它深深扎根于国家机关之中。据广泛报道，黑帮头目正在与塞尔维亚安全部门及高级政客合作。“学生名单”以“塞尔维亚或黑手党”为口号竞选，但打破国家与有组织犯罪之间的联系是危险的。一位尝试过此举的前总理佐兰·金吉奇，因之在2003年被暗杀。在某种程度上，武契奇的败选与欧尔班不同。匈牙利反对派由彼得·马扎尔领导，他是一位魅力十足、不知疲倦进行竞选活动的社交媒体台前人物。塞尔维亚的反对派则松散且去中心化。这曾是优势，但在执政后可能成为弱点。武契奇预测学生将崩溃，并预言自己将在两年内重新掌权。也许吧。但他们已向其他国家展示了击败强人的新方法。■

item.title: Poland is growing less religious, but not less right-wing

item.content:encoded:
Poland is growing less religious, but not less right-wing

Europe | Faith no more

Oct 29th 2026

For most of the day, Gabriela’s classroom in Wroclaw, a city in south-western Poland, is a hive of activity. But on Thursdays, as religion class starts, most of the kids trickle away. Religion lessons are optional and limited to one hour a week, but even that is sometimes too much for 12-year-old Gabriela, who says she envies the kids who get to opt out. Of the 18 pupils in her class, only three take religion.

Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries, with 92% of adults identifying as Catholic. But religiosity is declining. The share of adults who do not practise at all has doubled in under a decade, to 22%. Sunday Mass attendance has fallen from 45% in 2005 to below 30%. Church weddings, baptisms and priest numbers have dropped, and the church has been forced to look abroad for recruits. At a seminary in Kielce, in southern Poland, nearly a third of the trainee priests are from Africa.

The exodus is especially acute among the young. From the 1990s, when Poland scrapped communism, until the early 2010s the share of secondary-schoolers in their final year who took religion courses hovered around 90%. By last year it had dipped to 35% (see chart). The share who are non-believers is 24%, four times the figure for adults. Youngsters everywhere tend to be less religious than their parents, but in Poland the generation gap is unusually wide. “Secularisation here is happening faster than anywhere else,” says Andrzej Kobylinski, an academic and priest.

One factor is economic growth, which tends to boost secularism. Poland’s record on that front is extraordinary: GDP per head, adjusted for purchasing power, has quadrupled in two decades, propelling the country to about the same real income level as Spain. Meanwhile, a rash of clerical sexual-abuse scandals in the late 2010s tarnished the church’s reputation.

Another element was an informal alliance between church leaders and the right-wing populist Law and Justice (PiS) party, which governed from 2015-23. That alienated many youngsters, and women of all ages: hundreds of thousands protested in 2020 after the constitutional court, dominated by PiS appointees, imposed an almost total ban on abortion. Covid left a mark, too. Attendance at mass plummeted during the lockdowns, and has not recovered. Support for abortion and same-sex marriage has risen in the past decade.

But a more liberal society has not always made for liberal policies. Donald Tusk, the prime minister, heads a government spanning centrists, progressives, leftists and conservatives. During his campaign in 2023 he pledged to ease the abortion ban, but splits in his coalition have prevented that. A ruling by the European Union’s top court has forced Poland to accept gay marriages conducted abroad, but the country’s own laws have no provision even for same-sex civil unions. In July the president, a PiS ally, vetoed legislation that would have granted some rights to same-sex partners.

Rather than weakening the conservative opposition, secularisation is reshaping it. The Konfederacja (KWiN) party is challenging PiS as Poland’s main opposition. Although many of its politicians are Catholic hardliners, KWiN’s agenda pays little attention to the church. It focuses mainly on Euroscepticism, manosphere vibes, low taxes and stopping migration.

“Secularisation is not a threat to the right,” says Krzysztof Bosak, KWiN’s co-leader. Religion takes up “a very small fraction of our overall political message”. That may explain the party’s appeal among the young and religiously indifferent. Polls suggest it enjoys more support from the young than any other party.

Meanwhile PiS has seen its support fall to under 20%. In hopes of winning back voters from KWiN and the Confederation of the Polish Crown, an even more extreme (and often antisemitic) far-right group, PiS this year picked a nationalist Catholic as its candidate for prime minister. But that alienated the party’s moderates. In July a group of 40 MPs headed by Mateusz Morawiecki, a former prime minister, left PiS to form a new centre-right grouping, Development Plus.

In the past, says Aleks Szczerbiak of the University of Sussex, the conservative recipe for success in Poland was to be “left-wing on economic issues, right-wing on moral and cultural issues, and very religious”. That formula has expired, he says. Now the right’s binding force is no longer faith but fear—whether of immigrants, woke culture or the EU. Mr Kobylinski says this mirrors developments elsewhere in Europe, pointing to the secular, populist-right Alternative for Germany.

The good news for Mr Tusk is that with less than a year before a general election, his ruling Civic Coalition (KO) is in first place in the polls. The bad news for him is that KO and its allies lack the votes to form a government. For now, PiS and the far right together have a big enough share to form a majority. The right is deeply divided; in the last campaign KWiN vowed never to rule with PiS. But should they overcome their differences and take office, it would be as a more secular yet more extreme right-wing force than ever.■

item.content:encoded:
欧洲最大的钢铁厂可能即将走到尽头

欧洲 | 钢铁还是肺 2026年10月29日

20世纪70年代，位于意大利南部海岸塔兰托的钢铁厂曾是欧洲最大的钢铁厂之一，拥有2万名工人，每年生产数百万吨钢铁。如今，该工厂员工已缩减至8000人，并于本月停产。7月，米兰一家法院下令其于10月25日前关闭以安装污染控制设备。业主提出上诉，意大利总理焦尔吉娅·梅洛尼（Giorgia Meloni）政府允许其保持熔炉温度，以便恢复生产。本周，意大利最高法院将决定是否必须关闭熔炉，这可能意味着该厂的终结。

钢铁厂的烟囱高耸于城市上空，喷吐着毒素。在附近的坦布里区，居民每天都要清扫阳台上的红色粉尘。研究记录显示，癌症和呼吸系统疾病发病率升高，儿童认知能力下降。一项研究发现，2011年至2019年间，该工厂附近有超过1000例超额死亡；另一项研究发现，肺癌死亡率比地区平均水平高出30%。当地儿科医生格拉齐亚·帕里西（Grazia Parisi）表示，她看到越来越多的儿童患有呼吸系统疾病和结膜炎。她的病人包括患有白血病和脑肿瘤的儿童。当孩子咳嗽时，母亲们会担心最坏的情况。帕里西医生说：“我们害怕呼吸、害怕吃东西，也不敢让孩子们在田野里玩耍。”

起诉该工厂的人中包括奥雷利奥·雷布齐（Aurelio Rebuzzi），他的儿子亚历山德罗（Alessandro）患有囊性纤维化，16岁时去世。在工厂附近的教堂里，在耶稣手指钢铁厂的马赛克画像下，雷布齐先生回忆说，医生曾敦促他把儿子带走。“但亚历山德罗拒绝了，他说：‘不该离开我所爱的城市的人是我，而是那些来污染它的人。’”

政府担心关闭工厂会损害意大利制造商，并摧毁塔兰托的经济。该工厂于1964年开业时归国家所有，1995年被私有化，但一直难以应对国际竞争和法院对污染的处罚。国家一再介入，对该厂进行赔偿和纾困。10月中旬，工人们封锁道路以抗议关闭。在该厂工作了26年的工会组织者奥龙佐·斯帕纽洛（Oronzo Spagnulo）表示，政府应该在保留就业机会的同时使炼钢更清洁。他的父亲也曾在该厂工作，死于脑癌。工人们努力在生计与健康之间寻求平衡。安全官员安杰洛·比基耶里（Angelo Bicchieri）说，不在工厂工作的居民认为工人们是同谋：“他们恨我们。”

环境智库Ecco表示，该厂可以从煤炭转向天然气，再转向绿色氢能，成本约为110亿欧元（120亿美元）。但员工人数将缩减至3200人。政府表示可以获得欧洲绿色协议基金，并希望找到新的私人投资者来资助其余部分。但关闭令使该厂吸引力下降。一些居民甚至拒绝清洁钢铁的想法。他们更希望该地区停止炼钢，转向农业和旅游业。过去二十年，欧洲钢铁产量缩减了三分之一。如果塔兰托钢铁厂顺应这一趋势，也许并非坏事。

item.content:encoded:
又一列致命火车事故令西班牙基础设施受到质疑

欧洲 | 西班牙铁路 2026年10月29日 今年第二次，西班牙乡间横七竖八地躺着被压碎的火车车厢。10月28日上午，国营铁路公司Renfe运营的一列高速列车在托莱多以南追尾一列停着的列车。至少68人丧生，58人重伤。幸存者描述了Renfe列车首节车厢和由意大利控制的竞争对手Iryo运营的停驶列车后三节车厢内的骇人惨状。今年1月，同一条线路上发生了类似悲剧，一列Iryo列车脱轨后被一列Renfe列车撞击，造成46人遇难。在此之前，西班牙高铁网络——仅次于中国的世界第二长高铁网——是国民自豪感的来源。如今西班牙人感到震惊。社会党首相佩德罗·桑切斯在事故现场说，一年内发生两起严重铁路事故“在一个像西班牙这样的国家是不可接受的”。“整个西班牙都在悲痛之中。”

本周的事故发生在控制线路信号的连续自动列车控制系统停止工作之后。列车一度停运。但交通管制员下令Renfe列车恢复行驶，这一决定被交通大臣奥斯卡·普恩特称为“无法解释”，17分钟后便酿成致命后果。保守派反对党领袖阿尔贝托·努涅斯·费霍表示：“西班牙有权知道其基础设施出了什么问题。”桑切斯承诺展开调查。但在西班牙，调查往往拖沓且没有定论。警方的一份报告将1月的事故归咎于轨道维修缺陷，但尚未得到证实。2021年铁路网络自由化导致客流量大幅增加。批评政府的人士表示，维护支出的增长未能跟上。还有人表示，Renfe和国营铁路基础设施公司Adif都塞满了政治任命的人。大选定于11月29日举行；在为期三天的官方哀悼期间，大多数候选人已暂停竞选活动。很快，西班牙人将作出裁决，看看他们责怪谁。■

item.description:

欧洲 | 最终版 2026年10月29日 莫斯科市中心一座巨大的现代主义建筑，曾是印刷厂，挂着一块朴素的名牌：Novaya Gazeta（新报）。记者们正在打包书籍、物品、回忆。纸板的沙沙声和胶带的刺耳声。新闻编辑室里堆满了箱子，上方是一块路牌：“波利特科夫斯卡娅广场”，以安娜·波利特科夫斯卡娅命名，她是该报的著名记者，20年前的本月遇害。一名年轻员工在其他人休息时坐到他们旁边，只是为了和同事们多待一会儿。一辆手推车沿走廊驶过，载着照片印刷品。“仿佛我的一生都过去了，”该报的会计说。一位垂头丧气的摄像师记录着俄罗斯最后一家自由主义媒体机构的最后时光。 德米特里·穆拉托夫（图中人物）是《新报》...
item.content:encoded:
克里姆林宫正在关闭俄罗斯最后一份自由报纸

欧洲 | 最终版 2026年10月29日

莫斯科市中心一座巨大的现代主义建筑，曾是印刷厂，挂着一块朴素的名牌：Novaya Gazeta（新报）。记者们正在打包书籍、物品、回忆。纸板的沙沙声和胶带的刺耳声。新闻编辑室里堆满了箱子，上方是一块路牌：“波利特科夫斯卡娅广场”，以安娜·波利特科夫斯卡娅命名，她是该报的著名记者，20年前的本月遇害。一名年轻员工在其他人休息时坐到他们旁边，只是为了和同事们多待一会儿。一辆手推车沿走廊驶过，载着照片印刷品。“仿佛我的一生都过去了，”该报的会计说。一位垂头丧气的摄像师记录着俄罗斯最后一家自由主义媒体机构的最后时光。

德米特里·穆拉托夫（图中人物）是《新报》的出版人，也是诺贝尔和平奖得主。10月19日，他在前往巴黎纪念波利特科夫斯卡娅遇害的途中，得知报社被逐出已占用三十年的办公楼。其资金渠道也将被封锁，因为被贴上了“外国代理人”的标签。次日，他得知总编辑谢尔盖·索科洛夫被拘留并接受讯问。10月26日，穆拉托夫和索科洛夫召集报社剩余员工到隔壁大楼的地下室，让他们把手机留在外面。前一晚有人闯入报社办公室，在那里谈话不安全。穆拉托夫解释说，这是升级的迹象。他们可能被宣布为极端组织，其“成员”可能被捕。员工们同意是时候关闭这家创办于1993年的报纸了——那一年俄罗斯通过了后苏联宪法。“我们没有死，是他们杀了我们——连同宪法一起，”穆拉托夫说。“你只能对宪法第29条发笑：‘禁止审查’。”

在一个由军国主义独裁统治的国家，一家独立反战报纸的关闭并不令人惊讶。令人震惊的是，在弗拉基米尔·普京发动全面入侵乌克兰并使俄罗斯与西方隔绝之后，它竟然坚持了近五年。其许可证被吊销，网站被封锁，但它继续报道，找到越来越巧妙的方式接触读者。

早在20世纪90年代末的车臣战争期间，《新报》的记者们就开始揭露国家对自己人民的暴力，而那场战争确保了普京对权力的掌控。该报有六名记者被杀害，其中包括波利特科夫斯卡娅。“我恨普京，”她在2004年写道，“因为他的冷嘲热讽……因为无休止的战争……因为谎言。”她警告说，俄罗斯正在走向法西斯主义。2006年10月7日，普京生日那天，她在进入公寓楼时被枪杀。

战争迟早会来，穆拉托夫说：“当人民被当作尘土对待、制度被摧毁时，暴力必然蔓延到我们的国界之外。”正是《新报》揭露了2014年在顿巴斯作战的是俄罗斯正规军，而非 rogue 分离主义者。该报率先报道瓦格纳雇佣军集团由叶夫根尼·普里戈任控制，后者后来发动了反对普京的兵变，并在不久后死于飞机失事。2018年，普里戈任曾向报社办公室送去葬礼花圈和砍下的公羊头。

在普京下令入侵乌克兰的第二天，《新报》以俄语和乌克兰语两种语言出版，标题为“俄罗斯。炸弹。乌克兰。”几天后，克里姆林宫将“战争”一词定为犯罪并实施事实上的军事审查，该报出版了一期，头版标题为“无话可说”，后面是空白纸张。当发行商停止向报摊配送时，读者来到编辑室买光了全部印数。

入侵后，该报三分之二的编辑人员移居拉脱维亚，创办了《新报欧洲版》。穆拉托夫和其他约30人决定留在莫斯科。由于无法报道乌克兰战争，他们报道了战争在俄罗斯的后果：政治犯、经济恶化、心理创伤和审查。一些年轻记者加入了。“给我一份工作吧，”一位年轻女性申请时说。“任何主题，任何事情——我只需要一个我能大声说出我反对的地方。”

这家报纸为那些反对战争但不愿离开俄罗斯的人提供了安慰和尊严。普通莫斯科人去那里是为了不感到孤独。“那是一个让你感到身处正常世界的地方，一个罪犯不被奉为英雄的地方，”一位记者说。

但即使在普京加大对乌克兰城市的攻击之际，他也在摧毁俄罗斯境内仅存的少数自由公共空间。《新报》“是我们的城市，”穆拉托夫说。“他们摧毁了这座城市，我们正在离开。但我们不会放弃我们的工作。”他将把该报的许多纪念物品捐赠给读者，或如他所说的“同谋者”。

10月29日，斯大林主义镇压受害者纪念日，记者们开始朗读一长串当前政治犯的名字。一块来自索洛维茨基岛的石头——最早的古拉格集中营之一所在地——被放置在“安娜的花园”里，那是他们为纪念波利特科夫斯卡娅而在大楼前种植的一片绿地。■

item.title: 欧洲正在为一场俄罗斯早已发动的未来战争做准备
item.description:
Europe

item.content:encoded:
欧洲正在为一场俄罗斯早已发动的未来战争做准备

欧洲 | 查理曼 2026年10月29日 1939年9月法国和英国正式对德国宣战后的八个月里，令人瞩目的是几乎没发生什么事。这段时期后来被称为“假战争”：一个奇特的间歇期，西欧人声称在打仗，实际上却过着和平生活。（可惜，这样的日子并不长久。）如今欧洲面临的困境恰恰相反。理论上，乌克兰以西的欧洲大陆没有任何部分与俄罗斯处于战争状态。但和平已今非昔比。月复一月，克里姆林宫雇用的傀儡用无人机骚扰欧洲机场，破坏铁路线，纵火烧购物中心，威胁防务公司高管，入侵计算机系统，并在社交网络上散布瓦解士气的虚假信息。这一切都不构成常规战争——但也感觉不像非战争。不妨称之为“假和平”。俄罗斯让欧洲长期处于失衡状态，展现出太多好战姿态而无法忽视，却又不足以引发直接报复。借用一句俄罗斯谚语，战争与和平曾经是互斥的。如今在欧洲，它们同时并存。这带来了一个两难困境：欧洲究竟该为未来入侵的威胁担忧多少，又该为当前侵略的现实担忧多少？一方面，欧洲大陆正在为一场列夫·托尔斯泰可能认得出来的、针对俄罗斯的老式战争做准备——涉及火炮和部队调动（如今还有导弹和无人机）。另一方面，它已经卷入了一场不同性质的冲突，一场以破坏和宣传为武器的冲突。危险在于，欧洲专注于俄罗斯明天可能发动的硬战争——那种将军们毕生职业生涯都在准备应对的界线分明的战争——却忽视了已经全面展开的更为模糊的战争。目前，欧洲的大部分注意力都集中在坦克越境的威胁上。这并不令人意外：各国情报官员认为，俄罗斯可能试图在2030年之前对北约领土发动入侵。因此，军事物资正在订购，士兵正在训练，营级部队正在相应部署。国防预算大幅飙升以应对这一挑战。2022年之前，大多数北约国家的国防开支都未达到GDP的2%的目标。如今它们（大多）有望达到修订后的3.5%的目标。关于这新增的数十亿欧元应如何花费，争论激烈。欧洲国家应该继续购买美国武器，还是投入更多资金自主研发？坦克过时了吗？这类权衡取舍最好留给那些对榴弹炮了如指掌的人去决定。有些投资既有助于抵御常规威胁，也有助于抵御非常规威胁。以无人机为例，它既是乌克兰战争中的突破性武器，也是俄罗斯对欧洲其他地区发动低烈度攻击时使用的武器。学会应对无人机，无论在未来战场上还是在当今更模糊的局势中——无人机入侵已成家常便饭——都将带来丰厚回报。关于购买什么装备的争论有可能掩盖一个更广泛的问题：国防开支与更广泛的安全开支之间应如何合理分配？那笔占GDP 3.5%的巨额开支，其构想主要是围绕领土征服战争的风险，而这种战争即使对反复无常的弗拉基米尔·普京来说也显得鲁莽。俄罗斯花了五年时间试图打赢一场针对邻国的“三天战争”；再与北约较量将是一种奇怪的选择。与此同时，克里姆林宫已经在欧洲发动了一场某种意义上的战争。否则该如何称呼那源源不断的破坏和挑衅？荷兰机构国际反恐研究中心的研究人员记录了自2022年以来与俄罗斯有关的180多起此类事件。有些不过是通过互联网以几百欧元雇来的小混混干的升级版蓄意破坏。另一些则鲁莽至极，伤亡似乎迟早不可避免。2024年，藏在途经欧洲物流枢纽的包裹中的燃烧装置曾险些导致货机坠毁。今年8月，一枚装有炸药的无人机在德国莱比锡机场被发现。欧洲人并非没有意识到抵御所谓“灰色地带”战争的必要性。在承诺将GDP的3.5%用于国防的同时，北约成员国还承诺将GDP的1.5%用于更广泛的安全需求，包括保护关键基础设施、增强民事韧性等。但后一个目标定义松散，且主要涵盖现有支出。钱也不是唯一的障碍。领土防御虽然昂贵，但对军方人士来说是熟悉的领域，尽管由于无人机模糊了常规与非常规作战之间的界限，这一领域现在变得更加模糊。保护欧洲免受破坏和肮脏伎俩的侵害——既要威慑攻击，又要将影响降到最低——是一件更为棘手的事情。这通常需要警察部队、地方政府和私营企业协同合作。北欧国家长期以来一直认真对待此类事务。在德国，这些问题已进入公共讨论的视野。其他国家需要迎头赶上。这里的教训不是要削减安全支出——即用于应对低烈度侵略的支出——来成全领土防御。恰恰相反：正是因为北约的硬实力威慑如此可信，俄罗斯才诉诸非常规战争。欧洲需要更好地预防此类攻击，并在攻击得逞时最大限度地减少损害。但是，如何在避免危险升级的情况下反击俄罗斯——它往往否认自己策划了这些攻击？欧洲人有一个简单的方法可以向克里姆林宫表明，其恐吓运动是徒劳的。俄罗斯的许多恶意行为的最终目的是破坏欧洲对乌克兰的支持。11月，欧洲领导人将不得不就一项新的援助计划达成一致，以在乌克兰抵御入侵者的同时保持其偿付能力。一份慷慨的援助方案将传递出强烈的信号：俄罗斯的破坏不会让欧洲在对乌支持上动摇。当前的和平，尽管是虚假的，唯有以坚定的决心才能维持。■

item.title: 英国的防御性预算未能解决更深层次的问题
