item.title: India is pouring money and concrete into its border with China
item.description:
Asia

Asia | The road to deterrence Oct 22nd 2026 JUST 10km from India’s north-eastern border with China, the village of Zemithang lies in the heart of territory claimed by the Chinese. Everyday life feels unmistakably Indian. Locals chat in Hindi, listen to Bollywood songs and fly Indian flags. But o...
item.content:encoded:
India is pouring money and concrete into its border with China

Asia | The road to deterrence

Oct 22nd 2026

JUST 10km from India’s north-eastern border with China, the village of Zemithang lies in the heart of territory claimed by the Chinese. Everyday life feels unmistakably Indian. Locals chat in Hindi, listen to Bollywood songs and fly Indian flags. But occasionally there is an unwanted Chinese presence. “My phone keeps changing to Beijing time [two and a half hours ahead], because I lose my Indian network and pick up the Chinese one,” says a local official. His complaint captures the challenge facing India as it tries to transform its remote frontier, and match a massive infrastructure roll-out on the other side.

India is pouring concrete and money into Zemithang and other parts of Arunachal Pradesh (AP) to strengthen its hold over the Himalayan state. Home to fewer than 2m people, it is claimed by China, which calls it Zangnan, or southern Tibet. The state was also the main theatre of the only war between the two countries. In 1962 Chinese soldiers descended through the mountains, overran Indian forces and occupied parts of it. They eventually withdrew, but the defeat has ensured that relations have been edgy ever since.

Today the frontier is far calmer. The two armies face each other across the “line of actual control”, a disputed border that runs through spectacular mountains and valleys (see map). Barring a few scuffles, there has been no clash in AP since 1975. Even during hand-to-hand fighting in 2020 between Indian and Chinese troops in Galwan, 1,500km to the west, the border in AP remained quiet. But this is an ugly stability, says Ajai Shukla, a security analyst based in Delhi. The road to the border on the Indian side is lined with military camps: an estimated 90,000-120,000 troops are deployed in the region. In August local political groups alleged there had been Chinese intrusions near Taksing, in eastern AP, though India’s government dismissed the reports as rumours.

The fiercest contest is over infrastructure. For decades Indian officials eschewed building roads in AP, fearing it would give an invading Chinese army an easier route south. That is now considered a mistake: poor connectivity hindered India’s ability to supply its own troops and kept its citizens isolated. Meanwhile China built an extensive network of roads on its side, as well as hundreds of “dual-use” villages that combine civilian settlements with military infrastructure.

India is rushing to make amends. “Until the clashes in Galwan, India assumed that the relationship with China would improve in a linear fashion. That incident was a real wake-up call,” says Jabin Jacob of Shiv Nadar University. These days India regards connectivity as essential to deterrence. Much of the work is led by the defence ministry’s road-building arm, which has constructed hundreds of kilometres of roads in the region, including the Sela Tunnel, which keeps Tawang, the biggest town in the area, accessible even during winter.

The building drive extends far beyond roads. AP’s rivers have huge hydropower potential. To harness it, India is planning several dams, including its biggest-ever on the Upper Siang river. Securing the border also involves breathing more life into the settlements near it. Indian officials have become increasingly alarmed by satellite images revealing the rapid expansion of Chinese border villages. In 2023 the Indian government launched the Vibrant Villages Programme. Around 27bn rupees ($286m) has been set aside for projects in the state, 6% of the state’s GDP.

The aim is to stem migration from the region, draw people in, and improve administration. Much of the focus is on construction. But the army is also helping to turn the area into a tourist attraction (for Indians only), offering visitors access to border posts and history lessons on the 1962 war. At Bum La pass, at around 4,600 metres, soldiers accompany tourist groups right up to the frontier and lead chants of “Bharat Mata ki Jai” (”Victory to Mother India”) while facing the Chinese side.

All this is welcomed. The state has always been one of India’s poorer and more isolated corners, but in 2024-25 (the latest year for which data are available) its economy grew by 10%, the third-fastest rate in the country. Still, residents crave more development and of better quality. Locals fret that funding takes too long to arrive and gets tangled in bureaucracy.

Such complaints reflect the chasm between China and India that shapes their rivalry. China enjoys greater economic and military resources and also the advantage of unfettered state capacity. It is said to have forcibly relocated people to border villages. The Indians, meanwhile, must contend with local concerns—such as opposition to the construction of dams. ■

Stay on top of our India coverage by signing up to Essential India, our free weekly newsletter.

item.title: 印度人的权利数十年来不断遭到侵蚀

item.content:encoded:
印度人的权利数十年来不断遭到侵蚀

亚洲 | 阿育王 2026年10月22日

印度宪法充满了各种崇高理念。序言承诺每一位公民享有正义、自由和平等，更不必说尊严。正文部分设计了一系列令人眼花缭乱的制度来保障这些权利。然而，几乎在文件墨迹未干之时，印度的新领导人就开始改变主意。宪法第一修正案对言论自由权施加了“合理限制”。第24修正案明确议会甚至可以修改有关基本权利的部分。到1976年英迪拉·甘地实施紧急状态期间通过的第42修正案时，情况跌至谷底——议会不仅进一步限制印度人的权利，还创造了一种叫做“基本义务”的东西。紧急状态最终结束了，但对权利的侵蚀并未停止。历届政府都在削弱或架空独立机构。纳伦德拉·莫迪自2014年上台以来延续了这一跨党派传统。在他的统治下，许多人认为调查机构是其印度人民党（BJP）的执法臂膀，议会频繁形同橡皮图章，法院对维护个人自由也变得出奇地不感兴趣。

印度人在大多数情况下对此视而不见。对绝大多数人来说，有更紧迫的关切。然而，有一项权利印度人极其严肃地对待，那就是投票权。每五年他们走向投票站，在普遍被认为自由公正的大规模选举中表达赞同或不满。在两次选举之间，政客们专横跋扈，假装选民不存在，肆意挥霍公共资金。没关系。只要公民相信他们在选举日拥有惩罚统治者的权力，他们就能忍受很多。这就是印度社会契约的精髓。人们感到这一契约正在被践踏，这正是最近针对莫迪政府抗议活动触动神经的原因。

在该国近10亿登记选民中，约有1.3亿人被从选举名单上除名，这是一次“特别密集修订”，政府称其为“净化”名单中重复和已故人员所必需。批评者称这剥夺了数百万乃至数千万公民的选举权。这两种说法很可能都属实。上个月，《印度快报》披露，据称独立的印度选举委员会三名委员中有两人曾至少14次反对其首席专员加内什·库马尔主持下的决定。委员会否认了这一说法。但抗议者在10月大部分时间里走上街头，要求库马尔辞职，并把他描绘成印人党的傀儡。

早在特别修订之前，印人党就一个一个邦地使用卑鄙的政治手段及其对机构的控制来分裂对手政党并挖走其议员。选民们接受了这一点，就像他们曾经接受武装分子在该国更无法无天的地区 routinely 占领投票站、塞满选票一样。也就像他们仍然接受猖獗的买票行为——既有合法的（国家发放的现金补贴），也有非法的（候选人发放的现金）——一样。所有这些都被视为游戏的一部分。

现在争议的是一个更根本的问题：游戏本身是否已被操纵。印度的政治阶层应该认为自己很幸运。在邻国中国，共产党必须做的事情比赢得选举困难得多。中国的社会契约要求国家持续提高生活水平、生活质量和国家实力，作为交换，公民不干预政治。所有印度政客需要做的只是每五年假装对选民感兴趣一次。然而，莫迪政府不仅没有接受这笔划算的交易，反而通过镇压试图维护这一契约的抗议活动来加倍下注。

任何踏进过印度厨房的人都会熟悉高压锅，这是一种可怕的装置，它会在可预测的间隔发出巨大的嘶鸣声来释放积聚的蒸汽，与选举周期颇有几分相似。然而，如果这个通常的排气口被堵住，可能会发生两种情况之一：安全阀破裂，滚烫的蒸汽四处喷涌；或者压力不断增大——越来越大——直到发生灾难性的结构损坏。正是为了预防这样的爆炸，印度的缔造者才在宪法中加入了安全阀。把它们全部堵住不仅危险，而且是愚蠢的。■

item.title: 中国大学很有钱，但正面临压力
item.description:
China

中国 | 压力重重的大学 2026年10月22日 在与中国的竞争中，美国有时会自我破坏。在唐纳德·特朗普的领导下，联邦政府对大学支持的削减尤其具有破坏性。为了表达他们的痛苦，一些美国科学家提请注意他们的战略竞争对手可能从这些紧缩中获益的优势。去年，哈佛大学一位学者抱怨说，中国被“拱手送上银盘”般地获得了未来。在中国，从事共产党青睐的人工智能和机器人技术等前沿领域研究的学者有充足的资金。但这位哈佛学者可能会惊讶地发现，在许多校园里，教职工的情绪是阴郁的。尽管共产党热切希望推动科学事业，但在谁获得国家资金的问题上，它正变得越来越有选择性。今年4月，教育部表示，近年来已撤销了12,200个学位项目...
item.content:encoded:
中国大学很有钱，但正面临压力

中国 | 压力重重的大学 2026年10月22日

在与中国的竞争中，美国有时会自我破坏。在唐纳德·特朗普的领导下，联邦政府对大学支持的削减尤其具有破坏性。为了表达他们的痛苦，一些美国科学家提请注意他们的战略竞争对手可能从这些紧缩中获益的优势。去年，哈佛大学一位学者抱怨说，中国被“拱手送上银盘”般地获得了未来。在中国，从事共产党青睐的人工智能和机器人技术等前沿领域研究的学者有充足的资金。但这位哈佛学者可能会惊讶地发现，在许多校园里，教职工的情绪是阴郁的。尽管共产党热切希望推动科学事业，但在谁获得国家资金的问题上，它正变得越来越有选择性。今年4月，教育部表示，近年来已撤销了12,200个学位项目，主要是“工商管理”等软学科，代之以人工智能和共产党优先考虑的其他科学专业。但涉及物理和化学等学科的院系也感受到了压力。本十年中央和地方政府在科学技术上的支出年均仅增长3.5%，较2010年代末的10%大幅下降。这些支出涵盖从博物馆到社会科学的一切，但政府在自然科学系上的支出增长也在放缓。一些大学的预算正在被削减。今年9月，北京的北京大学是几所发布“厉行节约、过紧日子”新令的大学之一。在一些机构，研究人员的薪酬和福利正在被削减。自20世纪90年代以来，中国的大学迅速扩张，学术人员的生活条件变得舒适得多。该国大学的国际地位也大幅提升。根据英国杂志《泰晤士高等教育》的数据，2017年只有两所大学进入世界前100名。今年有八所，其中清华大学和北京大学分别位列全球第11位和第13位，是亚洲排名最高的。对于长期以来习惯了美好时光的中国学者来说，勒紧腰带带来了痛苦的冲击。即使是该国75所由中央政府资助的精英大学中，也有一些受到挤压。今年它们的预算中位数增长了6.8%，但有五分之一的学校遭遇削减。有些学校将研究生项目的奖学金数量和金额削减了一半以上。中国经济疲软是部分原因。除顶尖大学外，许多大学严重依赖地方政府的资金，而地方政府的预算正因房地产市场的长期低迷而受到压缩。地方政府负责该国2,900所大学中的95%。《经济学人》查阅的文件显示，即使在深圳和杭州这两个共产党支持的科技重镇，大学今年的预算也被削减了5%以上。经济仍在以4.5%的速度增长，但无法创造足够的新就业机会来吸收创纪录数量的毕业生：青年失业率为19%。因此，更多人选择留在校园。博士生的年招生量自2019年以来几乎翻了一番，达到20万人。留在学术界的人不得不竞争日益缩水的政府资金份额。博士后工作变得不稳定，正如一位学者所说，晋升要求正变得“不人道”。

学者通常需要获得资助才能晋升。自2021年以来，中国国家自然科学基金（中央政府科学资金的主要来源）主要资助项目的申请量已上升80%，达到20万份（见图表）。但发放金额仅增长了3%。申请成功率从2013年的22%降至去年的12%。今年，该基金会将给年轻研究人员的资助提高了50%——也许部分是为了平息他们的不满。恢复幸福感将很困难。约克大学的许强表示，中国的大学正越来越多地采用西方的雇佣方式，学者往往要辛苦多年才能获得永久职位。一些人抱怨说，由于预算紧张，大学正在招聘初级人员来加强研究，却无意给他们永久职位。如今，在学术界获得职位或晋升如此艰难，以至于许多人选择离开。深圳中学雇用了100多名拥有博士学位的员工。正如共产党的主要喉舌《人民日报》上个月指出的那样，中国的大学并没有“缺钱”。至少从总体上看，它们得到的更多：根据官方数据，去年大学研究支出增长了11%，达到3,410亿元人民币（470亿美元）。但企业，包括非国有企业，正在提供越来越多的资金。在有数据的最近一年2024年，企业提供了大学研究新资金的一半。但他们对支持不太可能培养出有助于商业发展的人才和技术的学术研究兴趣不大。而且他们更倾向于资金充足的名牌大学。

吝啬也许有些好处。普林斯顿大学的谢宇（他还在北京大学运营一个中心）表示，当中国大学快速扩张时，晋升往往与发表材料的数量而非质量挂钩。现在，注重资金的大学不得不更加挑剔，并产生更多突破。但正如一位学者指出的那样，发表论文的压力会助长欺诈行为。“论文工厂”在淘宝等热门电商网站上宣传他们的服务。一些研究人员因行贿发表作品而被抓获。网上侦探（包括博士辍学者）一直在挖掘学术不端行为，以将教授拉下马。一些省级政府正在调查一种做法，即学者付费让企业资助他们的研究，以满足晋升所需的资助配额。在一项小规模的政府调查中，五分之一的受访者承认有此行为。初级学者大多在长期就业前景不佳的情况下埋头研究。然而，一些人将登上学术之巅。正如在中国出口部门中那样，激烈的竞争可以帮助产生冠军式的想法。■

item.title: 中国想要重振长征精神

China

item.content:encoded:
中国想要重振长征精神

中国 | 长征 2026年10月22日

这是一个关于“坚韧、团结与希望”的故事。中国官方媒体本月发布的一部英文纪录片如此宣称，以纪念长征正式结束90周年——那场内战期间处境艰难的共产党人所进行的著名艰苦撤退。该系列片的两位外籍主持人重走了共产党所走过数千英里中的一小段，一路上说着些陈词滥调。“我们不仅看到了历史，也看到了未来，”其中一人感叹道，对红军曾经跋涉过的偏远地区如今涌现出的摩天大楼和数据中心赞叹不已。“总会有人走在通往希望的路上，”另一位在最后一集感慨道。有些人可能会觉得这有点过于煽情。幸运的是，中国本月还发布了第二部关于长征的纪录片，面向国内观众，更有意思。这部名为《伟大远征》的纪录片由中国人民解放军联合制作，在央视高调播出。它也歌颂了中国自上世纪30年代黑暗岁月以来的现代化成就。但它通过坦克、导弹和直升机的震撼画面来传达这一观点。这部纪录片的重点不是关于希望的废话，而是对党和领袖绝对忠诚的必要性。《伟大远征》的一个核心焦点是毛泽东，以及他在长征途中与其他共产党人的冲突，比如受过苏联训练的布尔什维克革命家博古、德国顾问奥托·布劳恩（李德），以及 rival 将领张国焘。他们在军事战略上与毛泽东有各种分歧。但正如纪录片津津乐道地讲述的那样，毛泽东一次又一次被证明是正确的。1935年初，博古和布劳恩被剥夺了指挥权；稍后，张国焘胆敢成立自己的中央委员会（党的最高领导机构），并带领他的部队朝着与毛泽东建议不同的方向前进。张国焘在一场灾难性的战斗后蒙羞；纪录片的镜头扫过他部下士兵的坟墓。在社交媒体上，一位热情的评论者总结了核心信息：“不知道怎么走，看看毛主席；遇到困难，再看看毛主席。”对今天党员的含义相当明确。毛泽东的继任者习近平的镜头出现在每集的开头几分钟。据官方媒体报道，该纪录片应“引导和激励全党全军……更加紧密地团结在以习近平同志为核心的党中央周围”。中国共产党的一亿多党员中，很多人都会收看《伟大远征》，如果他们知道什么对自己有利的话。它被放在一个名为“学习强国”的政党应用上，这个名称既意为“学习强大国家”，也意为“学习习近平使国家强大”。党员使用该应用的情况会被追踪；他们必须每天登录。军人尤其应该踊跃观看。近年来，数十名将军因不忠而被清洗。正如习近平所说：“每一代人有每一代人的长征。”每个人都应该跟上他的步伐。■

订阅者可以注册我们的新周报《鼓楼》，了解世界如何看待中国，以及中国如何看待世界。

item.title: China’s party elite gathers with purges and promotions in mind
item.description:
China

China | The fifth plenum Oct 22nd 2026 “Off-sites” at hotels are among the more sorrowful features of modern working life. Who does not dread the awkward conversation over the breakfast buffet, the unexpected grilling from the boss during a presentation or the struggle to stay awake through the ...
item.content:encoded:
China’s party elite gathers with purges and promotions in mind

China | The fifth plenum

Oct 22nd 2026

“Off-sites” at hotels are among the more sorrowful features of modern working life. Who does not dread the awkward conversation over the breakfast buffet, the unexpected grilling from the boss during a presentation or the struggle to stay awake through the post-lunch carb crash? Spare a thought, then, for the 300 or so members of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee who will soon attend one of the most brutal gatherings of the genre. The Soviet-style Jingxi Hotel in Beijing, where it takes place roughly once a year, is run by the armed forces. Mobile phones are thought to be banned, as are alcohol and cigarettes. Participants have to assume that every word is recorded by note-takers or bugs.

The “fifth plenum”, to be held from October 26th to 29th, will be especially fraught. It comes about one year before a quinquennial congress that is expected to give Xi Jinping a fourth term as the party’s leader. That means that he and other party bigwigs will be scrutinising potential candidates for promotion next year to the top decision-making bodies: the Politburo and its (now seven-strong) Standing Committee. What’s more, the theme of this year’s plenum is “full ​and rigorous party self-governance”—in other words, combating the corruption and indiscipline that continue to frustrate Mr Xi. So attendees’ personal conduct will be examined even more closely than usual.

Mr Xi might also spring a surprise, perhaps by floating proposals to adopt a new title such as party chairman (held by Mao Zedong). A plenum in 2016, also a year before a congress, established Mr Xi as the party’s “core leader”. That paved the way for him to scrap term limits on the presidency. And a year before a congress in 2022 another plenum further elevated his authority by granting his political doctrine equal status to those of Mao, Communist China’s founder, and Deng Xiaoping, the architect of reforms that began in 1979.

The plenum’s precise mechanics are secret. But based on limited official accounts of previous ones, it will start with Mr Xi delivering a report from the Politburo on its work over the preceding year. Next he will make a speech explaining the main item on the plenum’s agenda, in this case a “decision” on party self-governance. Participants are then expected to divide into about ten groups to discuss the report and the proposed decision. These breakout sessions usually include one each for military delegates, regional leaders and the chiefs of state-owned enterprises.

In the past the smaller meetings have sometimes involved fierce debate over ideology or policy. Not so under Mr Xi. Each delegate is expected to express approval of the party chief’s leadership, the Politburo’s report and the decision. But they must try to do so in pithy, creative terms while heeding Mr Xi’s increasingly dire warnings against self-promotion, flattery or performative parroting of party slogans. If they strike the right balance they might hope to get their remarks included in the note-takers’ summary of discussions, which is thought to be sent to top leaders at the end of each day. Better still is to catch the eye of Mr Xi, who usually drops into group talks in person along with other Standing Committee members.

On the last day the delegates reconvene and vote (unanimously, unless they are intent on career suicide) to confirm the expulsion of purged Central Committee members and to appoint replacements. That could reveal fresh victims of Mr Xi’s purges, which have already ensnared some 20 full members of this Central Committee, including three in the Politburo. Some of the committee’s members have already been replaced, leaving eight empty seats. Another 15 could be expelled, reckons the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), a think-tank in New York.

There could be signs that others are in trouble if they do not attend or are not promoted. And there may be new appointments to the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces (although that normally happens at a congress). The commission currently has just two members—Mr Xi and a general—following a purge of the other five.

Participants then vote (unanimously again) to approve the decision on party governance. It is expected to reinforce anti-corruption work with measures including closer oversight of government spending, enhanced use of big data and more accountability for officials whose subordinates break the party’s rules. It might also bolster the power of bodies that investigate errant officials. In a speech published (with omissions) on October 15th, Mr Xi said the party needed to “confine power to a cage of institutions”. He cited threats including “nice guys” who ignore problems, “two-faced” officials who secretly hold liberal views, and a “revolving door” between business and government.

Mr Xi’s goal appears to be to win support among the elite for his next five-year term and his quest to revitalise the party. If so, he is also revealing the limits of his powers to implement change, suggest Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang of ASPI. In a recent paper they compare Mr Xi to a Leninist Logan Roy, a patriarchal character in the TV series “Succession”. Like Logan, Mr Xi “presides over an enormous enterprise, exercises commanding authority and remains perpetually disappointed by the people expected to carry out his wishes”. In Mr Xi’s view, they add, there is only one model of diligence to emulate: that of his own younger self.■

Subscribers can sign up to Drum Tower, our new weekly newsletter, to understand what the world makes of China—and what China makes of the world.

item.title: 中国真的更看重AI速度而非安全吗？

item.content:encoded:
中国真的更看重AI速度而非安全吗？

中国 | 茶馆 2026年10月22日

“守住黄金三秒，守住你的钱包。”最近几周，一位慈祥的警察郭涛的视频在中国广泛传播，他发出了这一警告——提醒人们如何应对电话诈骗。只需一句简单的问候，犯罪分子就能捕捉到你的声音，然后用人工智能合成它来欺骗亲友。所以，正如郭先生所说，接到陌生号码来电时最好保持沉默三秒钟，看看是否是一个真人在说话。这个建议不错。它也涉及科技界最紧迫的问题之一：中国如何看待AI带来的风险？许多观察人士认为中国并不太在意这些危险。唐纳德·特朗普就是其中之一。“中国绝对不会阻碍AI的发展，”他上个月声称，以此解释自己对监管的不屑。事实上，调查显示中国对AI表现出压倒性的乐观态度。盖洛普的一项民调中，93%的中国受访者表示AI主要会对国家有帮助，而美国这一比例仅为36%。要求中国与美国合作减缓前沿模型发展的呼吁在北京被置之不理。“制造恐慌”对谁都没有好处，中国外交部表示。

事实上，中国花费了大量时间思考AI安全问题。电话诈骗只是各种担忧的冰山一角。中国的关切从犯罪活动、劳动力流失、国家安全，一直到——没错——让硅谷夜不能寐的失控场景。这并不令人意外。对生活中几乎每个领域的危险都执念颇深的共产党，多年来一直在努力将网络空间置于控制之下。一个将互联网视为生存挑战的政权，会突然放任AI肆意发展吗？如果像特朗普政府那样，将监管从本质上定义为一种减缓手段，那么中国实际上确实在减缓AI——尽管它从不会这么说。“中国已经拥有全球最严格的AI规则，”北京咨询公司Trivium的肯德拉·谢弗表示。基础性文件是中国的AI安全治理框架。第二次更新于9月发布。它列出了三大类下的54项风险：“固有”风险（模型以非预期方式行事）、“应用”风险（被犯罪分子利用）和“次生”风险（社会疏离）。它还提出了消除或至少减轻这些威胁的方法。其中之一是要求在检查点进行人工（还记得人类吗？）审查，并在必要时在AI代理过度扩散之前予以叫停。

该框架的一些早期想法已经付诸实施——例如，AI生成的内容（如音频和视频）必须明确标注。其他想法则可能构成新规的基础。征求意见稿要求服务提供商立即关闭存在严重问题的任何功能。10月16日，中国还提议限制其最先进AI技术的出口。随着AI变得更加强大，中国对末日情景的关注也越来越多。其安全框架的原始版本发布于2024年，仅对失控问题做了简单提及。而在最新版本中，这一话题出现了十多次。即便如此，仍能看出一种理念上的差异。美国有些人担心AI模型最终会超越人类智能并掌控自身进化，而中国更普遍的看法是，AI是一种可以被驾驭和引导的变革性技术，而非会脱离人类掌控的东西。习近平将AI比作蒸汽机、电力和互联网——这些技术具有划时代意义，但并不构成需要协同减速的危险。由于中国在AI前沿领域仍落后于美国，习近平更不可能同意踩刹车。在中国看来，这样的协议既无必要，也是美国人的自私之举。

不出所料，中国官员将大量精力投入到意识形态上。他们希望确保模型在重大问题上不与党相悖，确保新工具不会削弱其控制。但也有更多日常性的关切，反映了中国国家温和的家长式作风。因此有了郭涛在电话中的“黄金三秒”，以及禁止向未成年人提供虚拟恋人或虚拟亲属的规定。中国对规则的热衷可能会产生意想不到的效果。在美国，政府干预较少，企业便主动填补空白，评估自身模型并要求更多护栏。而在中国，企业往往较为被动，在应用管控措施之前等待党和政府的指示。北京咨询公司Concordia AI对十家近期发布模型的中国企业进行审查后发现，只有五家发布了安全评估。这表明，如果模型发展速度超过监管者预期，可能会出现危险。

对于那些认为中国开源权重模型不可避免具有危险性的人来说，中国的规则也无法打动他们。批评者担心，与在美国占主导地位的闭源模型不同，这类模型更容易被滥用。然而，中国AI界的许多人认为好处大于风险：他们指出，中国的开源模型帮助保护计算机系统免受美国闭源模型发起的恶意攻击，例如OpenAI工具曾攻破AI平台Hugging Face。无论如何，中国已经在制定更严格的规则来管理开源模型。业内人士表示，新发布的模型在向公众提供之前要经过严格的安全审查。以大多数衡量标准来看，中国的AI模型在性能上落后美国几个月甚至更久。对于一项快速演化的技术来说，这是一个巨大的差距。但不要指责中国在风险管理方面落后于美国。在规则、管控、限制和警告方面，中国正可谓如鱼得水。■

item.content:encoded:
Republicans’ identity crisis in Texas

United States | Midterms maths

Oct 22nd 2026

REPUBLICANS IN AMERICA’S biggest red state don’t usually have to play defence. But less than two weeks before election day, they are panicking. Ken Paxton, the scandal-plagued Senate candidate, is trailing James Talarico in the polls. Since early September, national Republicans have poured about $200m into ads in a bid to save his campaign—and their Senate majority. Greg Abbott, Texas’s three-term governor, has won past elections by double digits, but this year is being forced to fend off a Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, outspending her six-to-one over the summer. “We’re worried about Texas,” Donald Trump admitted early this month.

Mr Paxton is a uniquely bad candidate, dogged by investigations and marital infidelity. But he is not Republicans’ only problem in Texas. Latinos in South Texas, who swung to Mr Trump in 2024, now appear to be drifting left; soccer moms in the suburbs of Dallas and Houston are tired of the president’s rancour. After more than two decades of unbroken rule, Texas Republicans are struggling to find a winning message—old campaign lines aren’t working and the party is trying to whip up the base by questioning if foreigners belong. Even if the party hangs on to power in Texas on November 3rd, its grip is loosening.

Like Republican candidates elsewhere, those in Texas are being dragged down by Mr Trump. The president’s statewide approval rating is -18, according to The Economist’s tracker. Mr Paxton told donors in September that Mr Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas sank his numbers, according to a leaked recording. Mr Abbott was conspicuously absent from a Trump rally in San Antonio on October 7th.

Texas’s political identity has long been secure enough to withstand a national leftward tilt. Now Republicans’ Lone Star arguments are losing force. For years, calls for border security united Texas Republicans and won over many independents. The party can now boast that the problem has been fixed—border encounters in August were 94% below the average month under Joe Biden. The issue is also less salient. For the first time in a decade, voters rank the cost of living above immigration as the “biggest issue facing the state”.

The ferocity of Washington’s deportation crackdown doesn’t help. “Stephen Miller and the guys calling shots in DC have taken immigration policy from being a net positive for Texas Republicans and made it neutral or negative,” says Bill Miller, a Republican lobbyist in the state. After a federal agent killed a man in Houston in July, Mr Paxton offered no condolences.

When the going gets tough, Texas Republicans tend to fall back on bragging about the “Texas miracle”, the economic boom unleashed by low taxes and light regulation. In the five years to 2025, at least 184 companies moved to Austin, Dallas and Houston. When Google announced a $40bn investment last November, Mr Abbott declared the state the “headquarter of headquarters” and promised to make it the “epicentre of AI development”.

Those words now haunt him. This year Texans, like Americans elsewhere, turned against data centres, forcing Mr Abbott to ask the legislature to repeal the tax breaks that helped lure them. Ms Hinojosa, his challenger, pounced on the hypocrisy. Campaigning in towns such as Amarillo and Granbury, where Democrats rarely win, she casts herself as a populist. “Greg Abbott is selling you out,” an ad reads. The governor’s other big policy priority, universal school vouchers, is also unpopular among Republicans in small towns, where public schools are a top employer.

“The classic arguments have run out of steam and a new order hasn’t been born yet,” says James Henson, an Austin pollster. To fill the void, some Republicans are testing a new message that they hope will resonate in November and beyond: “keeping Texas, Texas”. The meaning of that slogan has recently come into focus, as politicians wage war on foreign influences they say threaten Texas from within.

First it was Muslims. Last year Mr Abbott tried to block a mosque in Plano from building a community he dubbed “Sharia city” and designated America’s biggest Muslim civil-rights group a terrorist organisation. Mr Paxton tried, unsuccessfully, to bar Muslim schools from school vouchers. In the Republican primary Mr Paxton beat John Cornyn, the incumbent senator, with the help of an endorsement of Mr Trump and a new line of attack, with ads accusing Mr Cornyn of having a “special place in his heart for radical Islam”.

Then it was legal immigrants. In January, Mr Abbott froze H-1B visa applications at state agencies and universities. Four months later Mr Paxton opened investigations into 30 firms he accused of using “ghost offices” to allow “foreign nationals to invade Texas”. In September Bo French, a Republican running for railroad commissioner (a job that actually involves regulating oil and gas), posted a photo of students celebrating a University of Texas football victory on X—nearly all of whom had brown skin. “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” he wrote. Old-guard Republicans whom the party has ostracised, including Karl Rove and Mr Cornyn, called the post racist. Texas’s top brass didn’t condemn it.

The fight over who belongs in Texas is most heated in the suburbs. There, dizzying growth has transformed Republican strongholds into political battlegrounds that decide statewide elections. Between 2020 and 2025, the Dallas metro area grew faster than any other in America. The Muslim population grew with it, building cultural centres the size of Walmarts, and the share of people who identify as Hindu roughly tripled. In Frisco, a wealthy northern suburb where a quarter of residents are now Asian, city council meetings turned into political theatre. In public sessions this spring, speakers likened a proposed mosque to a Nazi recruitment centre and called Indians “job stealers”.

The effort fell flat. When a mayoral candidate in Frisco ran on the nativist message in June, he lost by 16 points. “The problems are manufactured in Frisco, and in a lot of other places too,” says Bill Woodard, a former city councillor. The fearmongering, he argues, jars with people’s positive experience of their neighbours. Burt Thakur, the council’s first Indian-American member and a former Trump voter, agrees. “It’s the consultant class doing what they do best,” he says, “which is cleave on during election times and try to figure out how to get out the vote.” Polls from the University of Texas show that social issues don’t resonate when petrol prices are high.

Mr Abbott is still expected to be re-elected and Mr Paxton may eke out a win, too—he is reviving a tactic that has worked for Republicans before, saying Mr Talarico, who once said “God is non-binary”, is for “they/them, not you”. But, as national Republicans search for a post-Trump direction, the bitterly fought campaigns in Texas offer a warning. “Texas is the design shop for the future of the party,” says Ross Hunt, a Republican strategist in Dallas. Some Texas Republicans seem to relish the divisive zeal that is Mr Trump’s speciality, but they haven’t convinced voters—beyond the 7% who vote in their primary—that they care about them and their problems. “If we can see that attitude get punished a little bit,” Mr Hunt says, “I don’t think anyone will shed a tear.”■

item.content:encoded:
中期选举筹款数据揭示了一个出人意料的故事

美国 | 绿色浪潮 2026年10月22日 共和党本该在今年国会选举中拥有两大优势：选区和资金。但这两者似乎都无法保护他们免受中期选举的血洗。尽管赢得了本轮众议院选区划分之战，并受益于偏向共和党的参议院战场，但民调显示，共和党目前在两院都处于落后。新的筹款数据也应打破保守派的希望，即该党候选人可以通过在竞选最后几周用广告淹没对手来缩小差距。第三季度财务报告显示，除了民调中的蓝色浪潮外，还有一股民主党资金的“绿色浪潮”。不包括自筹资金，共和党参议员候选人在7月至9月仅筹集了6500万美元，而对手则高达2.76亿美元。民主党在众议院筹款方面也拥有较小但仍具压倒性的优势，以2.26亿美元对1.3亿美元领先。 共和党通过独立“超级政治行动委员会”的大幅支出优势来弥补这些缺口，这些委员会不受捐款上限限制。仅埃隆·马斯克一人在第三季度就向此类组织捐赠了超过2亿美元。总体而言，倾向共和党的超级政治行动委员会在参议院广告上的支出以7.5亿美元对3.17亿美元超过了民主党。然而，这些团体为广告支付的费用大约是竞选团队自身的三倍，这使得民主党在直接筹款上的优势更有价值。因此，根据卫斯理媒体项目数据库，在10月上半月，支持共和党的参议院广告仅比支持民主党的多20%。此外，金钱不仅是竞选成功的原因，也是成功的衡量标准。候选人在本州从个人（捐款上限为3500美元）筹集的资金越多，他们就越有可能拥有大量热情的支持者。候选人质量不能仅从捐款比例来估算：现任议员通常比挑战者筹集更多资金，两党都在自己的选举大本营拥有巨大的筹款优势。但当候选人的捐款份额远高于你根据这些因素预期时，他们往往会在选举日表现超常。以此衡量，民主党在几乎所有竞争激烈的参议院选举中都拥有巨大的筹款领先优势。最极端的例子是堪萨斯州，该州自1932年以来从未选出过民主党参议员。《经济学人》的预测模型认为，在今年的政治环境下，一名普通民主党人在堪萨斯州试图击败共和党现任议员时，应获得该州个人捐款约三分之一。然而，牧师兼首次参选者亚当·汉密尔顿却惊人地获得了92%。在另外两场参议院选举中，提名人在夏季发生了变化，因此直到最近才获得新候选人的筹款数据。在缅因州，民主党人取代了被指控性侵犯的格雷厄姆·普拉特纳，支持前州议员特洛伊·杰克逊。在南卡罗来纳州，现任议员林赛·格雷厄姆去世后，共和党人提名了他的妹妹、政治新手达琳。民主党在这些选举中表现非常出色：他们的每位候选人都获得了该州约85%的捐款。唯一一场共和党拥有明显筹款优势的竞争性参议院选举是明尼苏达州。前体育解说员米歇尔·塔福娅在与民主党副州长佩吉·弗拉纳根的竞选中获得了该州54%的捐款——比浅蓝州在看似深蓝年份的基准高出19个百分点。果然，明尼苏达州在民调中看起来也具有竞争力。今年民主党的筹款优势并不新鲜。在过去四个国会选举周期中，该党参议员候选人的平均表现比我们模型的基准高出12个百分点。然而，特朗普时代的筹款数据仍然可靠地识别出了某个政党后来超出预期的州。本轮周期，跟进资金流向让堪萨斯州和明尼苏达州成为近期记忆中可能性最小的战场州这一民调结果更加可信。 ■ 通过《美国简报》（我们的每日通讯，快速分析最重要的政治新闻）和《制衡》（每周评论，审视美国民主状况和对选民重要的问题），随时了解美国政治。

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Why Gen-Z conservatives love Richard Nixon

United States | Nixon now

Oct 22nd 2026

To looksmaxxing and gymmaxxing now add Nixonmaxxing, an activity to stretch your thinking if not enhance it. Slickly edited videos featuring America’s 37th president, often set to hip-hop beats, have gone viral in recent months. Influencers are donning baseball caps and tote bags embroidered with slogans like “Pretty Girls for Nixon” and “Nixon Now More Than Ever”. Attendance at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library in California is up 30% on last year.

The strange revival of the disgraced late president owes much to the media-savvy millennials running the Richard Nixon Foundation, a non-profit that helps manage the presidential library and, in a newer development, pumps out bite-sized videos. Covering everything from his musings on America’s relationship with Russia to his thoughts on his rivalry with John F. Kennedy, the clips have racked up millions of views. “Love seeing these old Nixon videos resurface”, reads one comment. “They really show the younger generations what a political genius he really was.” Your correspondent, a forlorn Nelson Rockefellermaxxer, recently spent hours scrolling through content to figure out what’s behind the newfound love for Tricky Dick.

Few are hyping up detente or Nixon’s creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. In Gen-Z speak, the enthusiasm is mostly down to vibes. The most popular clips capture Nixon’s bare-knuckle politics and refusal to give up. Some young conservatives see in Nixon an analogue to Donald Trump: two presidents marked by their antagonistic relationships with the press and hounded by investigators. “The Right’s rediscovery of Richard Nixon is not about particular policies,” wrote Chris Rufo, a millennial conservative, on X recently; it’s about “the attitude, and the narrative of the self-made man who won 49 states on behalf of the Silent Majority, and was taken down in a Deep State coup.”

The Trump administration seems to have a similar view. The Department of Justice is reviewing whether the special prosecutor’s office that investigated the Watergate break-in committed misconduct. “If Watergate happened tomorrow it would be like a 12-hour news story,” quipped J.D. Vance, the vice-president, during a talk at the Nixon library in June. “The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.”

In embracing Nixon, young right-wingers are also rejecting their elders’ worship of Ronald Reagan. The Gipper’s faith in free markets and internationalism is at odds with the MAGA worldview. “Reagan is the baby-boomer god,” says Curt Mills of the American Conservative, a magazine. “And the subtext of so much of what the New Right and younger conservatives think is that old people destroyed this country, and if Reagan is their god, then it must be a false god.”

Alas for keepers of the Nixon flame, he remains one of most unpopular presidents in the country’s history. A burst of Nixonmaxxing is unlikely to fix his reputation anytime soon. Then again, he has been written off before. ■

item.content:encoded:
The curious, predictable case of the fake poll

United States | Fake numbers

Oct 22nd 2026

By late June, Mallory McMorrow’s campaign to be Michigan’s next senator was probably already doomed. The Democrat was squeezed between Abdul El-Sayed, a dynamic leftist, and Haley Stevens, an establishment-backed centrist, in a heated primary. When a poll was published showing she had the support of only 9% of registered voters, it seemed to be a death knell. Reporters asked when she would drop out, which she did on July 5th. It now seems that poll was fake.

An investigation published on October 20th by FiftyPlusOne, a data-journalism outfit, found that a group called Wedgewood Polls had fabricated its results. The discovery follows another in August, when the Los Angeles Times spotted a forged poll on the city’s mayoral candidates. FiftyPlusOne has also criticised a pollster for manipulating figures to serve its client. The spate of bad polls undermines an industry already widely distrusted.

Wedgewood published 15 public polls ahead of the midterm elections. Then FiftyPlusOne—led by G. Elliott Morris, a former journalist at The Economist—received a tip that the data were fake. Mr Morris and his colleagues confirmed the forgery by comparing Wedgewood’s figures with data from a provider the firm had supposedly employed. Mismatched identification numbers gave the scammers away. When FiftyPlusOne requested a comment from Wedgewood, the firm claimed it had forged the polls to “demonstrate the vulnerabilities” of the industry.

Whatever Wedgewood’s motive, there are many reasons to fake polls. One is to earn easy money by selling fraudulent services to campaigns and political groups, which tend to spend heavily on public-opinion research; another is to manipulate prediction markets, where billions are bet on elections. Fake polls can also be used to influence elections themselves, for example by making candidates seem unviable. Ms McMorrow claims that donations dried up after the fraudulent poll was published.

With so much cash coursing through elections in America, the incentives to fake polls are greater than in other democracies. However, oversight is weaker. In Brazil, South Korea and France, for instance, pollsters must submit information to national authorities that monitor their work. In August the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court upheld a R$53,000 ($10,600) fine for a polling firm that had released insufficient information about a poll, despite there being no suggestion that its results were misleading. America’s wild-west approach has benefits—the industry is more dynamic and understanding of public opinion is deep. But the country’s pollsters already faced public scepticism. The latest fiasco won’t help.■

item.content:encoded:
如何分享人工智能带来的财富？阿拉斯加提供经验

美国 | 引发分歧的股息 2026年10月22日

十月在阿拉斯加是个热闹非凡的月份。广袤的土地上色彩斑斓，白昼变得珍贵，肥硕的熊在冬季来临前匆匆增重。这也是阿拉斯加人领取报酬的月份。每年十月，州政府会将石油收入的投资收益以股息形式发放给居民。金额每年不同，但今年十月，每位在州内居住满一个完整日历年的居民将获得1200美元。半个世纪以来，阿拉斯加一直在进行一项实验，探索如何将其丰富的石油资源收入用于公共福祉。如今，美国立法者正在纠结是否以及如何分享人工智能可能创造的财富，该州的经验有了新的借鉴意义。有人提议将人工智能公司的股份投入公共基金，用收益支付股息或资助公共服务，这与阿拉斯加的做法如出一辙。但阿拉斯加的永久基金及其股息既提供了一个范本，也提供了一个警示故事。

该州的好运始于1968年，当时钻井工人在阿拉斯加北坡的普拉德霍湾钻探时发现了石油。不到十年后，阿拉斯加人投票决定设立永久基金，将一部分年度矿产特许权使用费投入这一投资工具。共和党州长迈克·邓利维表示，这一想法是“确保石油开采等有限资源能够转化为阿拉斯加人民的无限收入”。1980年，州立法机构成立了一家独立的州立公司来管理永久基金的投资。两年后，阿拉斯加开始发放股息。如今，该基金价值900亿美元，相当于每位阿拉斯加居民约12.2万美元。剩余的矿产特许权使用费以及石油生产税则用于资助公共服务。

很长一段时间里，这些财富似乎取之不尽。1969年的一次租赁销售就筹集了该州年度预算五倍以上的资金。1980年，阿拉斯加立法者废除了州个人所得税。此后，他们一直避免对居民征收其他广泛税种。这使阿拉斯加在美国石油州中独树一帜。德克萨斯和新墨西哥等其他州仍会征收销售税或所得税来为开支提供资金。

阿拉斯加对石油的完全依赖使其沦为油价波动的“人质”。2018年，在经历数年拮据之后，立法者首次决定动用永久基金收益来帮助维持州政府运转。如今，每年从基金中提取的资金约占州预算的三分之二。立法者必须在股息和公共服务之间争夺石油资金的分配。阿拉斯加大学安克雷奇分校经济学家布雷特·沃森表示，阿拉斯加的预算编制已变得“零和博弈”。

邓利维在2018年当选时承诺恢复一项长期存在的公式，将股息与基金投资收益挂钩，那样阿拉斯加人每年可获得超过3000美元的付款。但立法者早在两年前就因预算危机而停止遵循该公式。上任后，邓利维不得不面对现实；他任内的平均股息约为1500美元。共和党州参议院主席加里·史蒂文斯解释说：“每个当选时说‘我保证给你3000美元股息’的立法者，一旦到了朱诺，看着那份预算，就会意识到做不到。”

在邓利维的领导下，立法者还削减了服务支出，既是为了平衡账目，也是为了保留资金用于股息。由于缺乏州政府资金，各城市和自治市只能靠微薄的预算运转。非营利组织阿拉斯加市政联盟的尼尔斯·安德烈亚森表示：“许多地方政府……在钱花完后就直接关门了。”立法者长期以来一直希望股息能留住居民；如今一些人担心服务恶化会把人赶走。自2013年以来，该州每年净移民都为负值。

与伊朗的战争提供了一剂权宜之计：油价上涨支撑了州预算。共和党州长候选人伯纳黛特·威尔逊呼吁发放更大的股息支票；她的对手、前民主党州立法者乔纳森·克雷斯-汤普金斯则赞成财政改革。

至于人工智能财富，辩论才刚刚开始。佛蒙特州参议员伯尼·桑德斯希望大型人工智能公司将其50%的股份交给一只主权财富基金，该基金每年向美国人支付至少1000美元，并最终支持医疗保健和其他服务。OpenAI和Anthropic的老板们则倾向于将更温和的5%股份捐给公共基金。OpenAI还支持提高资本利得税和企业所得税。人工智能基金最初不会面临与阿拉斯加永久基金相同的财政压力：毕竟，美国仍征收联邦所得税。但阿拉斯加的困境表明，过度依赖单一收入来源的危险，以及股息如何轻易成为政治足球。唐纳德·特朗普已经在抛出一个与人工智能无关的“特朗普股息”，前提是共和党赢得中期选举。他最近恳求道，只要投票给该党候选人，“你们每人将获得5000美元”。■

通过我们的每日通讯《美国简报》（快速分析最重要政治新闻）和每周通讯《制衡》（审视美国民主状况及对选民重要议题），了解美国政坛最新动态。

item.title: City-hall socialists try to make populism pragmatic
item.description:
United States

United States | Mayors of America, unite! Oct 22nd 2026 ON A SWELTERING October Sunday in Los Angeles Nithya Raman, a city-council member running for mayor, laid out her vision for America’s second-largest city. Ms Raman (pictured) is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Y...
item.content:encoded:
City-hall socialists try to make populism pragmatic

United States | Mayors of America, unite!

Oct 22nd 2026

ON A SWELTERING October Sunday in Los Angeles Nithya Raman, a city-council member running for mayor, laid out her vision for America’s second-largest city. Ms Raman (pictured) is affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Yet the dream she described to Angelenos was not of “ending capitalist oligarchy”, part of the DSA’s platform, but of competence. “City government has made solving problems look impossible for so long, people are starting to believe it is impossible,” she lamented, before rhapsodising about homelessness audits and cutting red tape. Her slogan, far from being revolutionary, is simply: “A city that works”.

Donald Trump has long derided cities run by Democrats as crime-ridden hellscapes; it would seem a political gift that a growing number are either already led, or will soon be led, by Democratic Socialists, whom the president calls “crazed lunatics and radicals”. But even as Republicans try to use socialism to undermine Democrats’ appeal, a new crop of pragmatic city socialists insist they will do the opposite.

Zohran Mamdani of New York is the most famous of this group—even Mr Trump has proved unable to resist the magnetic mayor, holding a chummy press conference with him in September that enraged Republican strategists. But along with Mr Mamdani there is Katie Wilson, elected last year to be mayor of Seattle, as well as Janeese Lewis George, the Democratic nominee all but sure to be the mayor of Washington, DC. In LA Ms Raman is in a fierce campaign against the incumbent Democratic mayor, Karen Bass. These four are all millennials either aligned with, or members of, the DSA. All four have also, either of their own volition or pushed by external factors, inched to the centre. 

A pragmatic socialist may seem like an oxymoron, but America has a tradition of them. Mr Mamdani and Ms Wilson have spoken admiringly of the “sewer socialists” of 20th-century Milwaukee, who downplayed revolutionary rhetoric while trying to improve sanitation and parks. Today’s leftists have rebranded this strategy as “sidewalk socialism” or “pothole politics”. Ms Raman, for example, is fixated on repairing broken streetlights, a symbol of LA’s dysfunction. Unlike DSA members in Congress, who specialise in bold, inconsequential positions, socialist mayors must contend with their cities’ problems.

This does not mean abandoning populism. Mr Mamdani is rolling out a tax on pieds-à-terre—earlier this year he posted a video celebrating the prospect of a new levy on the $238m penthouse of Ken Griffin, a hedge fund boss. But more basic concerns are the priority.

Take public safety. Even progressive voters doubt the logic of abolishing the police, as the DSA has suggested. Ms Lewis George once wanted to cut police funding; now she highlights her career as a prosecutor and promises to “support law enforcement”. Mr Mamdani kept his predecessor’s competent police commissioner, Jessica Tisch, and continues to stand by her despite her status as a DSA bête noire. “He knows that allowing crime and disorder to spiral out of control would take New Yorkers’ focus away from his affordability message,” explains John Ketcham of the Manhattan Institute, a conservative think-tank.

On housing, the four speak as ardently about slashing red tape as they do about squeezing landlords. Mr Mamdani’s efforts have earned the praise of local developers. In LA Ms Raman is an urban planner who embraced the YIMBY movement while serving on the city council. She wants to reform a “mansion tax” she once championed, as it has helped depress development. Her about-face impressed Dave Rand, a land-use lawyer who represents developers. “I don’t want an ideologue,” he notes. “I want someone who’s going to adjust to the facts on the ground.”

In Seattle, Ms Wilson campaigned on new taxes on capital gains and vacant properties. But her proposed budget would plug the deficit, cut city jobs and increase police spending. The business lobby cheered. Democratic socialists “may have values that are anti-capitalist”, says Joe Nguyen, of the Seattle Metro Chamber, “but they exist in a capitalist regime”. Ms Wilson is forthright about her evolution from activist to politician. “I’ve had to do a lot of work this year building relationships with the business community that I didn’t necessarily need to have, or cultivate, as an organiser,” she admits. “As the mayor, everyone’s problems are my problems.”

A less charitable interpretation is that leftist mayoral candidates are better at promising than governing. Mr Mamdani made fast, free buses a centre of his campaign. One year on, he’s focusing on the fast. Ms Lewis George’s ambitious plans for Washington are running into the reality of the city’s dismal finances, flagging economy and limits under federal law.

If these shifts come as a relief to business leaders, they can outrage the base. This month The Stranger, a newspaper in Seattle, asked: “Is mayor Katie Wilson still a socialist?” Israel and Palestine have little to do with municipal governance, but Mr Mamdani’s criticisms of the war in Gaza energised progressive voters during his campaign. When he attended a vigil for the Israeli victims of the October 7th attacks, protesters heckled the mayor and called him a “traitor”.

Some members of the DSA’s chapter in LA reckon Ms Raman is insufficiently anti-Israel, too, and are suspicious of her support for market-rate housing. During a recent meeting at a church in Hollywood, every other DSA candidate on the ballot got louder cheers. A young woman next to The Economist placed a blank canvassing sign-up form under her pew. “I’m not interested in campaigning for Democrats,” she explained. A century ago Milwaukee’s sewer socialists were derided by other leftists for their “bourgeois” worries. But the concerns were real. And those other leftists remained on the fringe.■

item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普应该喜欢这部关于伊丽莎白·霍姆斯的新纪录片

美国 | 列克星敦 2026年10月22日

“现实是什么？”在纳撒尼尔·菲尔德的新纪录片《你能看见一切》的开头附近，身败名裂的企业家伊丽莎白·霍姆斯问道。这部纪录片讲述的是2023年她因欺诈罪入狱服刑前，菲尔德与她共度的34天。而观众心想：哦不，又来了。或者，至少那位对这场无休止的后现代时代感到厌倦的观众是这么想的——厌倦了被提醒客观真理难以捉摸，厌倦了被告知一个人对现实的把握取决于他选择相信哪一种叙事。

在这部巧妙而引人入胜的影片结尾，菲尔德和他的联合导演兰斯·奥本海姆不仅质疑了霍姆斯是否真的犯有欺诈投资者的罪行——她作为血液检测公司Theranos的创始人，声称自己革新了数十种疾病的检测方法。他们还对霍姆斯伴侣的动机、《纽约时报》的诚信，甚至他们自己对霍姆斯的描绘提出了质疑。你无法看见一切。那么你怎么能相信任何东西？

美国人早已接受了这一课。他们也许并非都读过米歇尔·福柯关于权力如何塑造真理的著作，或让·鲍德里亚关于现代媒体如何抹去真实与虚假界限的论述。（列克星敦也没读过。）但他们看过大量真人秀电视节目，对真理的可塑性已经变得足够老练，以至于选出了他们的第一位后现代总统，而且不是一次，是两次。或者说是三次？叙事各有不同。

矛盾的是，尽管这很符合自我拆台的学术圈特性，一场旨在颠覆传统权力结构的思想运动会帮助一位右翼美国政治家扩大了总统权力的范围。但从他早年谎报自己大楼的层数，到他作为真人秀明星的成功，再到他在白宫的岁月，唐纳德·特朗普展现了对这种腐蚀性的后启蒙现实观的直觉式掌握。他的商业和政治基本原则就是什么都不信，谁也不信。“我是一个不信任别人的人，”他在1990年对CBS新闻说。

特朗普的成功部分依赖于对其他政客以及新闻媒体、民调机构、法院和科学家所宣布的事实持有激进的怀疑态度。他知道，反射性的犬儒主义背后总是跟着它愚蠢的双胞胎——对与事实只有最脆弱联系的阴谋论的盲目轻信。否认选举结果的人、否认气候变化的人和反疫苗者正在美国的知识危机岁月中蓬勃发展。连地平论者都迎来了他们的高光时刻——如果民调可信的话，当然民调不可信。

平心而论，至少霍姆斯女士有理由对叙事的本质感到恼火或厌倦，尤其是新闻媒体构建的那种叙事。在她被广泛妖魔化之前，她曾受到广泛赞誉，包括在那些经过严格事实核查的出版物上。这种令人瞠目结舌的逆转发生在《华尔街日报》的报道揭露了Theranos开发的看似神奇的“爱迪生”设备无法执行霍姆斯声称的众多检测之后，她最终被判有罪。

正是在这一点上，菲尔德的纪录片聪明得过了头，对谁都没好处——也许除了霍姆斯女士。她给人的印象是一位和善的女士，只是有点古怪。当她把自己的幼儿和婴儿留给伴侣比利·埃文斯，开始为诈骗鲁珀特·默多克和沃尔玛财富继承人之类的人物服刑11年以上时，谁要是不同情她和她的家人，那简直是铁石心肠。

菲尔德提出了尖锐的问题，而且他是尴尬沉默的大师。但霍姆斯证明了自己与他旗鼓相当：她用沉默回应他的沉默，用睁大的、看似天真无邪的蓝眼睛回应他半闭的凝视，那双眼睛有时会泛起泪光。她说她相信自己从未说过谎，而且（与总统不同）她是一个信任别人的人，“总是做真实的自己”。菲尔德详细探讨了一种可能性：她的“欺诈”其实源于一场史诗级的沟通失误。当她说“爱迪生”设备“可以”工作时，她的意思是它将来可以工作，一旦科学赶上来。她没有欺骗任何人的意图。“她只是想法不同，”埃文斯解释说。

霍姆斯感叹道：“世界相信的关于我的现实并不是真实的。”后现代主义者是对的。权力确实塑造了对真理的感知，叙事确实可以塑造现实。霍姆斯的崛起证明了这一点。而且，正如特朗普所声称的，连法院都可能被操纵，陪审团也可能作出错误裁决。

然而，霍姆斯案中的陪审团似乎并非草率作出决定。经过近四个月的审判，陪审团裁定她四项罪名不成立，三项罪名悬而未决，同时裁定她四项罪名成立。他们仔细筛选了堆积如山的证人证词和书面证据，包括霍姆斯本人承认的事实：她在关于“爱迪生”的有利报告上亲自贴上了制药公司的标志，尽管这些公司根本没有得出这样的结论。

基于文字游戏而暗示陪审团可能判错了，这并不像一些影评人所说的那样，是“一次大胆的、也许不可能的求索真理”或“一场为真理本质而进行的战斗”。相反，这是对无法把握真理这一事实的一种耸肩——不是理想主义的斗争，而是投降，即便不是虚无主义。

也许为此感到激动是愚蠢的。这部电影发人深省而且有趣。但美国即将迎来又一次选举。如果结果不如特朗普的意，可以预料他会拒绝接受结果，甚至可能试图推翻结果。他以前就这么干过。美国人会效仿菲尔德和许多其他人的模式，举起双手，对事实到底是什么感到不确定吗？世界也许很快就会知道了。■

item.title: 卢拉如今处于劣势，还能再施妙手吗？
item.description:
The Americas

item.content:encoded:
卢拉如今处于劣势，还能再施妙手吗？

美洲｜巴西大选 2026年10月22日 10月25日的总统决选将成巴西自1985年回归民主以来最势均力敌的一次。本次选举的对阵双方是80岁的左翼现任总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦，以及前总统雅伊尔之子、45岁的弗拉维奥·博索纳罗。历史上，从未有在第一轮投票中落败的候选人最终赢得第二轮。不过，尽管卢拉在10月4日的第一轮投票中落后于弗拉维奥（卢拉得票45%，对手得票47%），他仍拒绝不战而降。他能上演逆转好戏吗？自第一轮落败以来，卢拉已采取戏剧性行动。他曾是一位连手机都不愿使用的技术恐惧者，近来却开始在Instagram上发布自拍视频。他公开支持降低严重犯罪行为的刑事责任年龄，而这一政策此前是左翼的禁忌。他还推动国会通过了一项极受欢迎的措施，将每周工作时间从44小时缩短至40小时，且不削减工资。他的竞选团队在大城市组织了数十万支持者参加的游行，其中不乏名人表演。他还在大笔承诺支出。他承诺免除理发师、美甲师或水管工等个体经营者累积的联邦税务债务，并向其中100万人发放1000美元。他承诺在周末提供免费公共交通。此外，政府最近还增加了旗舰项目对贫困家庭的现金转移支付，取消了巴西中下阶层民众的所得税，并决定取缔博彩公司（这些公司原本缴纳大量税款）。根据与巴西参议院有关联的研究机构独立财政研究所的数据，所有这些新措施合计可能使政府在2027年底前花费580亿美元（占GDP的2%以上）。这些承诺正在产生效果。卢拉正在缩小与博索纳罗的差距，尤其是在女性群体中。一些最新民调显示双方势均力敌（需注意巴西民调机构屡次未能完全捕捉右翼情绪，包括在10月4日第一轮投票前，当时民调显示卢拉领先）。10月10日之后的一周内，博彩公司几乎将卢拉的胜选赔率翻了一倍，但仍认为他落后于对手。博索纳罗正在反击。他此前曾嘲讽缩短每周工作时间，最终却投票支持了该法案。在10月18日的总统辩论中，他声称卢拉的第三个任期内犯罪率激增（实际上犯罪率有所下降）。在第一轮出局的四位右翼候选人共获得8%的选票，其中三人已表态支持博索纳罗。尽管民调差距缩小，总部位于巴黎的选举预测机构Le Millénaire仍将他的胜选概率定为82%。 探访巴西人口第二大州米纳斯吉拉斯州，可以看到卢拉需要翻越的高山。该州是巴西的缩影：其干旱的北部与卢拉的大本营、巴西贫困的东北部接壤。在南部和西部，农业综合企业和工业占据主导地位，选民倾向右翼。从未有总统在未赢得米纳斯的情况下胜选。尽管卢拉在2022年赢得了该州，但在10月4日他以五个百分点的差距输给了博索纳罗。在拥有25000人口的小镇蒙特西昂，约2000家微小企业在业主住宅底层生产针织品。居民抱怨生活成本不断上涨。在一家小企业的后屋，五名女缝纫工正在为连衣裙做最后修饰。“我们交这么多税，税，税，”其中一人抱怨道。“月底我们没有任何剩余——我们赚钱只是为了生存。”她的同事附和道：“这叫工人党，但工人什么也得不到！”她们的老板将沉重的利率归咎于债务增加。对卢拉的工人党（PT）的厌倦在这一地区很普遍，该党在过去24年中执政18年。在附近的波苏斯－迪卡尔达斯镇，那里以温泉和丰富稀土储量闻名，选民们感到沮丧。“卢拉说他会让所有人吃上皮卡尼亚（牛臀肉），但现在连鸡蛋都很贵，”一位45岁的泥瓦匠说，他指的是卢拉在2022年竞选中承诺让所有巴西人都富到能吃上顶级牛肉。他过去曾投票给卢拉，但他说这次将投空白票。在一个破败的郊区，64岁的理发师卡洛斯·莫伊塞斯正在清扫店门口的地板。他是一辈子的工人党选民，这次将投票给弗拉维奥，解释说自己被税压得喘不过气。“我知道博索纳罗家族不怎么样。但我们累了，你明白吗？”工人党建立在工会会员、天主教神父和学者的支持之上。它一直在努力适应一个更加福音派化的巴西，那里的工人越来越成为个体经营者。自2010年以来，登记的个体经营者数量从不到100万猛增至1500万。该行业如今占正式工作岗位的近五分之一。这些人通常收入太高无法获得政府补助，但又太低无法过上舒适的生活。多年来，工人党大佬们嘲笑他们为“一人公司的CEO”。卢拉免除他们部分债务的承诺是拉拢他们的迟来尝试。在绿色景观中散布着五旬节派教堂，有些宣扬庆祝财富的教义。“五旬节派的增长帮助在较贫穷社区传播了保守价值观，”28岁的圣保罗人卢卡斯·帕瓦纳托说，他刚刚为博索纳罗的政党赢得了一个国会席位。“左翼意识形态把一切都归咎于社会结构，而宗教则将改善生活的责任放在个人身上。”在福音派中，卢拉落后博索纳罗33个百分点。帕瓦纳托的成功证明了右翼在社交媒体上的实力。在10月4日举行的立法选举中，他获得的票数位居全国第二——仅次于尼古拉斯·费雷拉，一位拥有超过3000万粉丝的虔诚福音派基督徒和社交媒体达人。巴西人对社交媒体的使用比几乎其他任何地方的人都更多，许多人从这类平台获取新闻。在总统选举第一轮之前，博索纳罗的竞选团队至少花费200万美元在线上推广他的内容。卢拉的团队只花了大约50万美元，还发放了大量印有他头像的贴纸。最近，他的团队一直指责社交媒体平台不当限制其竞选信息触达。竞选时日所剩无几，卢拉的团队必须热切期望老办法仍可能被证明是最好的。■

item.title: 拉丁美洲正在拥抱以色列
item.description:
The Americas

美洲 | 比比在国外的伙伴们 2026年10月22日 “拉丁美洲正在发生一件了不起的事”，以色列四面楚歌的总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡在10月14日咧嘴笑道，“一切都回来了！伟大的友谊。”他是在哥伦比亚新大使馆于耶路撒冷开馆后发表上述言论的。哥伦比亚成为第四个承认这座圣城为以色列首都的拉丁美洲国家，也是迄今为止人口最多的一个。这很可能不会是最后一个。由于加沙战争，以色列变得更加孤立。然而拉丁美洲的保守派领导人——其中许多是新当选的——正在大幅加强双边关系。阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱最为热切。今年早些时候，他告诉《经济学人》，他认为内塔尼亚胡先生是一位“超级巨星”。他自己则奇怪地声称是“世界上最犹太复国...
item.content:encoded:
拉丁美洲正在拥抱以色列

美洲 | 比比在国外的伙伴们 2026年10月22日 “拉丁美洲正在发生一件了不起的事”，以色列四面楚歌的总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡在10月14日咧嘴笑道，“一切都回来了！伟大的友谊。”他是在哥伦比亚新大使馆于耶路撒冷开馆后发表上述言论的。哥伦比亚成为第四个承认这座圣城为以色列首都的拉丁美洲国家，也是迄今为止人口最多的一个。这很可能不会是最后一个。由于加沙战争，以色列变得更加孤立。然而拉丁美洲的保守派领导人——其中许多是新当选的——正在大幅加强双边关系。阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱最为热切。今年早些时候，他告诉《经济学人》，他认为内塔尼亚胡先生是一位“超级巨星”。他自己则奇怪地声称是“世界上最犹太复国主义的总统”。4月，米莱先生宣布了“以撒协议”，这是一个旨在加强以色列与该地区接触的模糊框架。布宜诺斯艾利斯与特拉维夫之间的新直飞航班将于下月开通。巴西总统选举的领先者弗拉维奥·博索纳罗誓言，如果他在10月25日获胜，将把巴西大使馆从特拉维夫迁至耶路撒冷。他在最近一次访问约旦河西岸时表达了对以色列定居者的“全力支持”；他和米莱先生都曾在西墙前祈祷。除了迁移大使馆外，哥伦比亚还在8月成为除美国以外唯一表示支持以色列对戈兰高地主张的国家。“我们从未如此关注与以色列的关系，”波哥大安第斯大学的桑德拉·博尔达表示。玻利维亚的罗德里戈·帕斯、智利的何塞·安东尼奥·卡斯特和洪都拉斯的纳斯里·阿斯富拉都加强了外交关系，而他们的前任曾因加沙流血事件而降低了这些关系。委内瑞拉临时总统德尔西·罗德里格斯软化了查韦斯政权长期以来对以色列的敌意。6月加拉加斯附近发生大地震后，她接受了以色列派遣救援队的提议，并恢复了领事关系。“拉丁美洲正在变成一个蓝色大陆，”哥伦比亚犹太社区联合会的马科斯·佩克尔说，他指的是以色列的蓝白国旗。该地区的一些领导人受到强烈个人信念的驱动。众所周知，米莱先生与一位拉比一起研读《托拉》。当《经济学人》8月访问他的办公室时，一张希伯来文文本放在他的桌上。在2025年对以色列议会的演讲中，他誓言要“捍卫西方文化”。然而，政治算计显然也是核心。向以色列靠拢是拉丁美洲新右翼讨好美国共和党以及唐纳德·特朗普的一种方式。伦敦智库查塔姆研究所的克里斯托弗·萨巴蒂尼表示，政治成本相对较低。民调机构皮尤的一项调查发现，略超过一半的阿根廷人、巴西人、哥伦比亚人和秘鲁人对以色列持负面看法——远低于英国报告的69%和西班牙的78%。在拉丁美洲大部分地区，与以色列和巴勒斯坦相关的问题对选民来说远不如打击犯罪和提振经济重要。该地区还有一个快速增长的群体鼓励对以色列的直言不讳的支持：福音派基督徒。许多人相信犹太人回归以色列应验了圣经预言。重生基督徒在推动右翼领导人上台方面发挥了有效作用。在哥伦比亚选举前，福音派选民为最终获胜者阿贝拉尔多·德·拉·埃斯普列拉举行了守夜祈祷，他曾是无神论者，现在是虔诚的天主教徒。福音派还在巴西选举第一轮中动员支持博索纳罗先生。该地区许多领导人上台时承诺对毒品团伙采取强硬路线。各国政府指望以色列的武器和建议来推动其计划。2022年，谋杀率是拉丁美洲平均水平三倍的厄瓜多尔表示将花费约6500万美元购买以色列装甲车。厄瓜多尔的暴力根源在于邻国哥伦比亚，德·拉·埃斯普列拉先生最近一直在那里轰炸武装团体。但阿尔贝托·何塞·梅希亚将军表示，武装部队需要以色列的情报和无人机技术才能有效行动，他曾在2015年至2018年领导哥伦比亚军队。2024年，时任总统古斯塔沃·佩特罗与以色列断交，并停止购买哥伦比亚军队长期依赖的武器和其他装备。梅希亚将军表示，该国的武器库存已经耗尽。哥伦比亚各叛乱团体现在聚集了超过2.8万名战斗人员，几乎是佩特罗先生2022年就职时的两倍。“以色列国防综合体将在这届政府身上大展拳脚，”一位哥伦比亚情报专家说。与以色列的亲密关系会持久吗？11月举行的美国中期选举与此相关。如果共和党人受挫，拉丁美洲领导人可能就不太愿意追随特朗普先生的领导。在智利，对以色列更友好的政策引发了反弹（该国拥有庞大的巴勒斯坦社群）。哥伦比亚以前支持巴勒斯坦政策的支持者 also 感到震惊。以色列自己的选举于10月27日举行，增加了不确定性。但至少就目前而言，拉丁美洲和以色列正享受着多年来最紧密的关系。■

item.content:encoded:
Rastafarians in Jamaica want more rights

The Americas | Herbal remedies

Oct 22nd 2026

SISTER NANNY is easy to spot. Sporting a red, gold and green dress—with a matching headpiece—the Rastafari campaigner is outlining an idea she thinks will help marginalised members of her faith. Jamaica takes advantage of the world’s interest in Rastas to “attract visitors” to the country, she notes. Yet those same people continue to suffer stigma. She thinks the Jamaican government should share proceeds with the community, whenever it profits from their culture.

Dreadlocks, cannabis, reggae: think of Jamaica and aspects of Rastafari culture commonly leap to mind. On the island, however, the religious movement has often been maligned. Rastafari beliefs originated in poor Jamaican neighbourhoods in the 1930s. They revolve around a single God, Jah, said to reside within each person. Haile Selassie I, the Ethiopian emperor crowned in 1930, is seen by some as the second coming of Christ (Selassie politely discouraged the idea).

From the beginning, authorities took a tough line. Many Rastafari were arrested for possessing cannabis, which they view as a sacrament. Schools and prisons forced them to shave their dreadlocks, which violates a vow. Violence erupted in 1963, following an altercation at a petrol station in the city of Montego Bay. Security forces detained Rastas all across Jamaica; some were killed.

In 2017 the Jamaican government formally apologised for the “Coral Gardens incident”, as it became known. This year it has gone further, formally handing the deeds to land in Montego Bay to a campaign group that Sister Nanny helps organise, as restitution. The land will be used for a Rastafari care home.

The move fits into a broader trend of pro-Rastafari policymaking in the Caribbean. In 2015 Jamaica somewhat liberalised its drug laws, explicitly permitting Rastas to grow and use cannabis for religious purposes. St Vincent & the Grenadines passed a similar rule in 2018; Barbados the following year. When Antigua & Barbuda joined them in 2023, the prime minister, Gaston Browne, acknowledged that his country had once tried to “destroy” the faith. This year St Kitts & Nevis formally recognised Rastafarianism as a religion, which grants it stronger legal protections.

Rastafari in Jamaica say discrimination has decreased, but not disappeared. “The police still harass Rastafari…for having herb,” says Ras Iyah V, chairman of the Westmoreland Hemp and Ganja Farmers’ Association. The movement is pleased with the progress, but it is pushing for more. Sister Nanny’s group has begun advocating for Rastas to get intellectual property rights that might protect “the colours, the language, the food...Anyone who wants to appropriate our culture, then they should pay”. The promise is that funds raised in this way would be used to build schools and more care homes.

Talks with Jamaica’s government continue. A lack of unity hampers the fight. In 2023 several distinct groups formed Rastafari Mansions and Organisations, an umbrella body, to help co-ordinate advocacy. Coherence remains a challenge, says Sister Nanny. “There is no one voice yet.” ■

item.title: Everything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Saudi bets gone bad Oct 22nd 2026 IN ANY OTHER year, Muhammad bin Salman would be getting ready for his star turn. October 26th was supposed to have been the start of the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual summit in the Saudi capital that is sometimes dubbed...
item.content:encoded:
Everything is going wrong for Muhammad bin Salman

Middle East & Africa | Saudi bets gone bad

Oct 22nd 2026

IN ANY OTHER year, Muhammad bin Salman would be getting ready for his star turn. October 26th was supposed to have been the start of the Future Investment Initiative (FII), an annual summit in the Saudi capital that is sometimes dubbed “Davos in the desert”. The crown prince usually spends the week glad-handing heads of state, titans of finance and other dignitaries, all of them eager to do business with his kingdom.

Not this year. The Houthis, an Iran-backed militia in Yemen, have spent weeks firing missiles and drones at Riyadh. The airport is still, in effect, shut after a series of deadly attacks. Many Western governments have warned their citizens not to travel to the kingdom. Executives were nervous that hotels or other venues could be targets. After days of deliberation, organisers decided on October 19th to postpone the event until next year.

As he rose to power a decade ago, Prince Muhammad made a few big gambles. He wagered that he could defeat the Houthis; that he could reshape the Saudi economy; and that Donald Trump would prove a reliable ally. All of them have gone awry at once. The decision to cancel FII is emblematic of Prince Muhammad’s annus horribilis. He faces a set of interlocking crises, none of which has a ready solution.

The Saudis failed to defeat the Houthis, but they had hoped a ceasefire agreed on in 2022 would contain the threat. Instead the truce began to unravel this summer because of America’s broader war with Iran. The Houthis have seized additional territory in Yemen and battered Saudi Arabia. People close to the crown prince see only bad options. The kingdom can send ground troops into a bloody war; continue a campaign of air strikes that is unlikely to succeed; or make a deal that helps cement the Houthis’ rule in Yemen.

A long conflict will derail the prince’s economic programme, which was sputtering even before 2026. Big projects were being shelved amid a strain on public finances. Wages have not kept pace with inflation. Annual foreign direct investment is only about one-third of the crown prince’s $100bn target. A year ago the IMF expected the Saudi economy to grow by 4% in 2026; now it expects a 3.3% contraction.

Whether it rebounds in 2027 will depend on whether peace breaks out in the Middle East—and that will depend largely on Mr Trump. The kingdom thought it had influence over him. It wooed him by promising to invest implausible sums in America. It also made tawdry deals with the first family, paying Trump-owned golf courses to host Saudi-funded tournaments and investing $2bn with Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law. None of that stopped Mr Trump from embarking on a disastrous war. “He’s not loyal to anyone for long,” says one well-connected Saudi.

There are no reliable public-opinion polls in the kingdom, but it is fair to say most Saudis trust their government. Some have found recent weeks unnerving, nonetheless: the war in Yemen has caused real disruption. Yet since October 10th, when a Houthi missile killed 13 people at Riyadh’s airport, Prince Muhammad has been largely invisible. It fell to ministers to visit victims and offer reassuring messages.

A few Western commentators have begun to ask whether this crisis-filled year poses an existential threat to the crown prince’s rule. The view among diplomats in Riyadh is that such talk is overblown. “He was in a much tougher place seven or eight years ago,” says one Western envoy.

Back then the prince was a newly appointed heir, still consolidating his rule. The war in Yemen was already a quagmire, the blockade of Qatar was upsetting America, and much of the world was horrified when Jamal Khashoggi, a Saudi journalist, was murdered inside the kingdom’s consulate in Istanbul. Prince Muhammad’s grip on power is far more secure today: he has sidelined rivals and centralised power unlike any Saudi ruler since King Abdulaziz, the founder of the modern state. Though he certainly has his detractors, none could plausibly organise a putsch.

Nor is he facing much criticism from allies. The response to the recent escalation in Yemen has been telling: even long-time critics of the war are now willing to acknowledge that the kingdom has little choice but to fight. “I do understand that this is a different moment than 2018 or 2020. They are facing these Houthi advances and Houthi rocket attacks,” says Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator who met the crown prince in Riyadh this month. “We should recognise that.”

Seen in another light, though, this is a more challenging moment for Prince Muhammad. Because the woes of his early years were mostly self-inflicted, they were easier to fix. By 2021 he was steering Saudi foreign policy in a more pragmatic direction. He ended the blockade of Qatar and sought a deal with the Houthis. Even the Biden administration, which took office promising to make the crown prince a “pariah”, grudgingly praised his new direction.

This year is harder. The biggest decision is out of Prince Muhammad’s hands. He has urged Mr Trump not to escalate the war with Iran. If the president ignores him and resumes bombing after the midterm elections in November, Saudi officials worry the kingdom will take blows from all sides: the Houthis to the south, Iraqi militias to the north and Iran itself to the east. They have a big country to protect—four times the size of France—and not many air-defence interceptors left to do it.

In his first decade, the crown prince made laudable strides towards liberalising Saudi society. Women can drive. Female labour-force participation has almost doubled. Concerts and cinemas are now widespread in a country where fun was long verboten. A few well-off foreigners can even enjoy a legal tipple. But the core of the Saudi state has changed little. Its economy still depends on oil money, its army is still built to protect the regime rather than wage war, and its foreign policy still relies on America as an indispensable protector.

Perhaps eventually those things will change as well. The Mecca pact, a mutual-defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkey, is an effort to find new allies that could supplant a now unreliable America. But those changes will take time. In his second decade, the test for Saudi Arabia’s ruler will be to change the foundations, not just the façade. ■

item.title: A deeply divided Israel prepares to vote
item.description:

Middle East & Africa | The more things change Oct 22nd 2026 On the morning of October 7th 2023 Hamas fighters drove through the Israeli town of Sderot, less than a mile from Gaza, shooting at civilians. For Israelis, the small city became a symbol of the extent to which their nation’s defenc...
item.content:encoded:
A deeply divided Israel prepares to vote

Middle East & Africa | The more things change

Oct 22nd 2026

On the morning of October 7th 2023 Hamas fighters drove through the Israeli town of Sderot, less than a mile from Gaza, shooting at civilians. For Israelis, the small city became a symbol of the extent to which their nation’s defences had failed. In the last election, in 2022, over three-quarters of its voters plumped for parties that joined the coalition government of Binyamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister. But nine days before the country’s next election, Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett, the leaders of the two big centre-right parties and Mr Netanyahu’s main challengers, were there to hold him to account.

Three years after the massacres of October 7th, Mr Netanyahu’s rivals are determined to make the election a reckoning for that day and the wars and bloodshed that have followed. “Whoever promises total victory is hoodwinking the public,” Mr Eisenkot said on his visit, in reference to Mr Netanyahu’s wartime slogan. “He has nothing to offer.” Those listening murmured in assent, but many more in Sderot still back the prime minister and his allies. Travelling around Israel, it is clear that the country is deeply divided. No party is set to win over 20% of the vote. Political alliances are shifting. Mr Netanyahu and his allies have no obvious route to power but his squabbling foes may not be able to form a coalition either.

Sderot is a hardscrabble “development town” in the Negev where in the 1950s Jewish immigrants from elsewhere in the Middle East, the mizrahim, were sent to live. Resentment towards what many there see as an elite dominated by Ashkenazi (European) Jews still lingers, fuelling votes for Mr Netanyahu’s Likud and its allies.

Sderot and towns like it are plastered with pictures of Mr Eisenkot with the slogan “A prime minister dialna”, an evocative word in Moroccan Arabic that means “of us”. If he wins, he will become the first prime minister descended from the mizrahi wave of immigration. Many Israelis would prefer him or Mr Bennett to lead the country. But the prime minister has beaten the polls and expectations time and again.

Twenty minutes down the road from Sderot is Netivot, another coalition stronghold. Most of the customers at a popular couscous joint reckon Mr Eisenkot is in the clutches of “the left”. Three contractors eating lunch all voted Likud in the past. But only one, Kfir Almassi, says he’s “sticking with Bibi”. The other two are disappointed with the inconclusive outcome of the Gaza war. “Bibi is too left-wing for me,” says another, Nave Cohen. He plans to vote for the Jewish Power party. Its leader, Itamar Ben-Gvir, currently the national-security minister, promises to make the population of Gaza “voluntarily migrate” if he remains part of the government. The third, Yaniv Magen, plans to vote for Yisrael Beiteinu, an opposition party led by Avigdor Lieberman, a nationalist who has sworn to remove Mr Netanyahu but, like others in the opposition, refuses to join a government supported by Arab-Israeli parties.

And yet splits among religious and right-wing voters threaten the prime minister’s grip on power. Netivot is a stronghold of Shas, the mizrahi ultra-Orthodox party led by Arye Deri, Mr Netanyahu’s oldest political ally. But a new Haredi party has sprung up there. It is unlikely to cross the electoral threshold of 3.25% but it could still deny Shas, and thus the Netanyahu bloc, a seat.

Another new party, the Haredi Public, is challenging the established ultra-Orthodox parties. These have long been close partners of Likud and the recipients of lavish public funding for religious schools that fail to teach subjects such as maths and science. The Haredi Public represents young ultra-Orthodox Jews who want their children to have the skills to join the workforce and even enlist in the Israel Defence Forces. “We probably won’t cross the threshold,” admits one activist at a packed rally in Jerusalem. “But we’re founding a movement to change our community and that’s more important.” Mr Netanyahu, worried that they, too, will cost his coalition seats, has tried—unsuccessfully—to persuade the Haredi Public to withdraw.

Meanwhile in the coffee-shops of Tel Aviv, Israel’s liberal bubble, secular Israelis feel the pressure to vote tactically. Some like The Democrats, a merger of the two struggling parties of the Zionist left, but reckon Mr Eisenkot’s Yashar is more likely to beat Mr Netanyahu, even if it is more right-wing than they would prefer.

Many who care about Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians feel politically homeless. “Neither The Democrats or Mr Eisenkot are addressing the conflict with the Palestinians,” says Sarah Ben-Yaakov. She’s leaning towards Ra’am, an Islamist party which in 2021 became the first independent Arab party to join a ruling coalition.

It is increasingly clear that the Arab parties could be the deciding factor in this election. In Kfar Qasim, an Arab town east of Tel Aviv, a large Likud billboard looms, warning of the danger of Mr Eisenkot joining Arab partners. “They put the sign there to make us despair of any chance to influence events and not vote,” says Issa Amer, an engineering student.

In 2022 only 53% of Arabs voted; general turnout was 71%. Pollsters expect many more Arabs will vote this time. The Arab parties could win more than their current ten seats. They might take seats from Mr Netanyahu’s bloc. But given the opposition’s qualms, they could make it harder for Mr Eisenkot to replace him. ■

item.content:encoded:
俄罗斯正在升级其在非洲的信息战

中东与非洲 | 宣传盛宴 2026年10月22日

10月28日，非洲领导人将齐聚莫斯科，参加自2019年以来的第三届俄罗斯-非洲峰会。对弗拉基米尔·普京而言，这一活动是他精心谋划的一部分，旨在说服全球南方，让它们相信俄罗斯是在代表他所称的“全球多数”反抗“新殖民主义”。自2022年俄罗斯全面入侵乌克兰以来，这一努力一直在加速。在2023年的最近一次峰会上，一位女发言人声称“俄罗斯男子在前线献出生命，以便非洲大陆的人民获得自由。”许多非洲领导人会对这种言论嗤之以鼻。但普京认为，非洲大陆为播撒俄罗斯的毒害思想提供了肥沃的土壤。今年2月，外交部长谢尔盖·拉夫罗夫表示，被欧洲驱逐的俄罗斯官员中有90%已被重新派往非洲大陆。俄罗斯加大了通过文化外交、东正教会、高等教育、专业团体、媒体企业和虚假信息来左右非洲民心的力度。与其在非洲大陆上更强势的军事干预一样，这种认知战的效果很难评估。但俄罗斯受益于人们对苏联挥之不去的同情，也受益于非洲对富裕国家的合理批评。俄罗斯的努力就像套娃：表面之下另有玄机。

以文化外交为例。今年9月，俄罗斯表示将把非洲的“俄罗斯之家”（隶属于外交部的文化机构）数量从16个增加到24个。批评者，如爱沙尼亚智库国际国防与安全中心的伊万·克雷什奇，称其为“俄罗斯宣传网络中的节点”。它们放映的电影支持克里姆林宫的叙事：《为非洲而战》——一部关于俄罗斯如何帮助萨赫勒国家反抗法国“新殖民主义”的纪录片，或《我为什么搬到俄罗斯》——讲述据称逃离本国“觉醒主义”的美国人的故事。乌克兰声称这些机构被用来招募非洲人加入对抗乌克兰的战争。欧洲各国政府正在辩论是否因其传播宣传而关闭各自境内的这些机构。

最新的俄罗斯之家于今年9月在圣多美和普林西比——一个曾是冷战时期苏联卫星国的葡萄牙前小小殖民地——开业，地点位于首都主干道上的一间原物理治疗诊所。入口处，一幅人工智能生成的拼贴画迎接着来访者，画面上是微笑的圣多美人和苏联口号“人民友谊”。负责运营该中心的因娜·阿法纳谢娃解释说，作家、君主、体育明星和宇航员的海报“讲述着俄罗斯的故事”。一张镶框的普京照片俯视着正在学习俄语的学生。

越来越多的非洲学生正在移居俄罗斯：最新统计约为3.7万人，大约是2010年的五倍，部分原因是奖学金增加。这一数字最近超过了冷战时期的峰值，当时苏联培养了一代非洲精英，包括现任安哥拉、加纳和纳米比亚总统。俄罗斯之家为曾在苏联留学的专业人士举办聚会，这是重新激活旧有关系努力的一部分。它们还为东正教会召集聚会。克里姆林宫支持教会在非洲的扩张——非洲有许多保守派基督徒——以将俄罗斯定位为传统价值观的避风港，而非一个所谓颓废的西方。

俄罗斯在非洲大陆推广媒体机构。国有媒体“今日俄罗斯”已与喀麦隆的非洲传媒等媒体达成内容共享协议。据法国政府去年发布的一份报告，2023年推出的“非洲倡议”声称是一家独立通讯社，但与瓦格纳集团（一支国家资助的俄罗斯雇佣军组织）的前成员以及俄罗斯情报机构有密切联系。该报告称，该组织是虚假故事的幕后黑手，这些故事指责美国在布基纳法索传播登革热，并且可能散布了法国支持困扰萨赫勒地区的圣战分子的说法。

与俄罗斯的许多努力一样，这伙人也与非洲创作者合作。由“非洲倡议”支持的马里甘地网络电视台有一档由马里主持人和一名俄罗斯记者主持的脱口秀节目。在布基纳法索，“俄罗斯时刻”由俄布混血说唱歌手MC鲁斯科夫主持。俄罗斯媒体正寻求影响非洲新闻业。自2025年7月以来，“今日俄罗斯”和其他国有媒体已为来自至少29个国家的非洲记者举办了至少20场培训活动。这些课程包含实用技巧，但材料带有偏见。乌克兰战俘被贴上“新纳粹”标签。乌克兰战争初期的布恰屠杀被用作需要事实核查的“假新闻”的例子。

其他谎言则通过线上线下相结合的运动被推动。今年，记者联盟“被禁故事”报道称，一个名为“公司”的俄罗斯支持的影响网络向整个全球南方的记者付钱，在当地媒体上发布假故事。举一个例子，该运动试图破坏洛比托走廊——一个由美国和欧盟资助的安哥拉基础设施项目。俄罗斯还制造假记者。在8月发布的一份报告中，非政府组织“非洲代码”和公司“Graphika”识别出多达35名拥有虚假资料的幽灵“记者”。他们的“文章”发表在真实媒体上，其内容又被其他媒体转载，形成“信息洗白”的循环。人工智能常被用来创建人物形象、撰写故事并翻译成当地语言。

“非洲代码”的贾斯汀·阿伦斯坦表示，类似的幽灵正出现在其他领域。他指出，假学者创建假学术研究并上传到预印本库，还有假智库发布报告，为俄罗斯的叙事增添可信度。俄罗斯努力的影响很难衡量。很少有非洲人观看“今日俄罗斯”或访问“非洲倡议”的网站。民调显示，平均而言，俄罗斯对非洲的积极影响被认为不如美国、中国或前殖民大国。这可能反映了俄罗斯在经济上能提供的东西较少。俄罗斯招募非洲士兵提醒人们其战争的真正代价，包括对非洲人的代价。然而，以此自慰是错误的。阿伦斯坦将俄罗斯运动的影响比作白蚁侵蚀非洲社会的结构。他说，克里姆林宫在虚假信息商贩中不同寻常，因为它故意试图削弱社会凝聚力，而不仅仅是推动自己的议程。毕竟，国家越脆弱，俄罗斯就越能利用它。■

订阅《分析非洲》周刊，让您随时了解这个世界上最年轻、也最不被理解的大陆的最新动态。

item.content:encoded:
约瑟夫·卡比拉向其继任者发难

中东与非洲 | 反了，反了 2026年10月22日 回到1974年，如今刚果民主共和国的首都金沙萨曾举办了一场奢华的拳击赛，被称为“丛林之战”。如今，这座城市正被另一场重量级对决所笼罩。一方是总统菲利克斯·齐塞克迪，另一方是前总统约瑟夫·卡比拉（如图）。10月12日，卡比拉震惊全国，宣布他将“以一切手段，包括使用武力”，领导一个反叛联盟对抗其继任者。卡比拉的举动可能加剧饱受战争蹂躏的东部地区的冲突，也使齐塞克迪试图修改宪法以在2028年第二任期结束后继续掌权的努力变得更加复杂。如果两人中任何一人能打出致命一击，都将影响这个非洲第二大国的未来——鉴于美国对关键矿产的渴求，这对其而言也事关重大。

两人的夙怨由来已久。最新篇章始于2019年，当时齐塞克迪在一场舞弊程度堪比巨型帆船的选举中被宣布获胜。事后，他与卡比拉达成权力分享协议，承认这位前总统在议会中的多数地位。2020年，该协议被激烈撕毁。卡比拉的忠诚支持者遭到清洗，卡比拉本人最终选择自我流亡，在私下里他向其他非洲领导人抱怨，认为自己被一个不合法的继任者夺权。

金沙萨的局势因东部的战火而更加紧张。2021年，得到卢旺达支持的反政府武装“M23”在沉寂八年后重新抬头，并于2025年初攻占了戈马和布卡武这两个地区首府。对于出生于东部的卡比拉来说，这场冲突是对其继任者“专制政权”的回应。而在2023年以争议较小方式赢得连任的齐塞克迪看来，这场战争是卢旺达的入侵。2025年卡比拉前往戈马时，齐塞克迪认为这证实了他的继任者是卢旺达的傀儡。2025年9月，刚果以叛国罪缺席判处卡比拉死刑。

接下来的一年里，卡比拉和M23否认有任何关联。“卡比拉不是我们的老板，”该组织政治分支的负责人科内耶·南加5月对《经济学人》表示。但现在他是了。卡比拉的联盟包括M23。他想利用东部的叛乱为金沙萨带来变革。

他能成功吗？戈马的非政府组织正在关注军队是否向富含矿产的加丹加地区南部移动。然而，M23的战士比其政治同僚更不愿扩大战场。卢旺达也没有表现出想要扩大冲突的迹象。它可能支持卡比拉的崛起，因为这会让跨境冲突看起来更像是刚果内部争斗。另一个参与者乌干达希望维持一项允许其在刚果东北部驻军的协议。美国今年已因卡比拉与M23的关联而对其实施制裁，因此不太可能欢迎任何破坏齐塞克迪政权稳定的努力——毕竟美国已与后者达成了矿产协议。

其他刚果反对派人物可能具有决定性作用。一个名为C64（以宪法第64条命名，而非1980年代流行的电脑）的松散联盟反对齐塞克迪争夺权力。一些人此前曾呼吁将卡比拉纳入“全国对话”。但现在支持他将更加困难。

卡比拉最大的希望可能是齐塞克迪被吓到，变得愈发多疑和专制。这可能引发战略失误——金沙萨一些人认为对卡比拉的死刑判决就是这样一个错误——并招致政治精英的强烈反弹。齐塞克迪已经面临压力。10月14日，比利时当局因一项洗钱调查搜查了他亲属的住宅。

这将相当于卡比拉采用1974年穆罕默德·阿里所使用的“倚绳战术”的政治版。阿里靠在绳上承受打击，让对手乔治·福尔曼挥拳至精疲力竭，然后打出致命一击。阿里显然说过：“如果你能兑现，这就不是吹牛。”刚果正在观望卡比拉是否也能兑现。■

订阅《解读非洲》周刊通讯，让您随时了解这个全球最年轻——也最不被理解——的大陆。

item.title: 法国的破坏与后果

item.content:encoded:
法国的破坏与后果

欧洲 | 骚乱与政治 2026年10月22日 在利摩日，19世纪市政厅的钟楼和屋顶在被纵火后坍塌。在马赛，打砸分子（casseurs）闯入了市政厅。在波尔多，蒙面的抢劫者砸碎了路易威登及附近商店的玻璃橱窗，抢走手提包、运动鞋和其他财物。电动滑板车堆成火堆，在街角燃烧。黑色浓烟滚滚升腾。全国范围内有超过2000人被逮捕。总统埃马纽埃尔·马克龙在电视讲话中宣称：“今晚我们都感到愤怒和羞耻。”随后他便启程前往海湾地区访问。法国对动荡并不陌生。但即使在一个对街头暴动习以为常的国家，10月17日的事件也令人震惊。是什么引发了这场破坏性的爆发？马克龙曾在2018至2019年间面对长达数月的“黄背心”暴力示威。然而，街头破坏与当局无力应对的组合更为糟糕。这体现了政府核心的瘫痪、中间派政治信心的崩溃，并为更大的分裂埋下伏笔：明年春季总统选举的选民可能面临民粹主义右翼玛丽娜·勒庞与民粹主义左翼让-吕克·梅朗雄之间的选择。

这场混乱是街头易燃混合因素——以及警力不足——的结果。内政部长洛朗·努涅斯承认警方“失去了控制”，议会调查已经启动。街头的人群分为三类。第一类是大约50万名学生、教师和工会成员，他们和平抗议教育投资不足和生活成本过高。“打砸分子正在败坏我们运动的名声，”20岁的大学生波利娜抱怨道。她说自己是在抗议“一切”——从拥挤的讲堂和昂贵的汽油价格到警方镇压。不受欢迎的总统也在她的名单上。“马克龙，你死定了”涂鸦出现在一个被砸毁的公交候车亭旁，旁边还有“ACAB”（意为“所有警察都是混蛋”）。

第二类人，即打砸分子，有混入示威活动的历史。他们身穿黑衣、头戴全罩式面罩，常常戴着滑雪镜和口罩，看起来就是要来打架的。2023年的一份议会报告称，法国此类极左团体（通常是反资本主义的无政府主义者）成员约有600至800人。他们身手敏捷、隐蔽性强，且善于躲避警察。2023年抗议后被捕的48名“黑群”成员中，85%是男性，75%年龄在33岁以下。报告指出，他们大多受过良好教育，并不贫困。时任巴黎警察局长努涅斯表示，他们寻求“制造麻烦以推翻体制”。第三类人是机会主义的抢劫者。TikTok上分享的信息引导年轻人前往被砸毁的店面。在波尔多，一名年轻男子漫不经心地把赃物晃进购物篮；另一些人则从鞋盒中取出抢来的耐克运动鞋，然后跑开。数小时内，赃物就被挂到网上出售——“示威期间偷来的毛衣”这样一条描述写道——随后网站将这些商品下架。约3000家商店和企业遭到抢劫或破坏。

情报部门曾预测参加人数为20万，而实际人数是这一数字的两倍多。部署的警察约6万名，比“黄背心”抗议最严重的时期少了约三分之一。在早前的抗议中，警方曾被指控施暴。而这一次，店主们对于自己被留下自生自灭感到愤怒。在总理塞巴斯蒂安·勒科尔尼授权在波尔多、巴黎、马赛和其他城市实施部分宵禁后，平静得以恢复。士兵将协助在计划于10月24日举行的下一轮抗议中维持秩序。

潜在紧张局势与正在使政治两极化的选举有关。执政近十年后，中间派的马克龙因宪法限制无法再次参选。许多抗议的学生对别的领导人治下的生活毫无记忆。法国想要改变，但对于接下来应该发生什么，社会严重分裂。梅朗雄的支持者参加了巴黎的示威，他们将这些抗议视为其旗手的一次力量展示。此前，69%的法国人在一项民调中表示支持抗议者，而在其支持者中这一比例升至92%。他的“不屈法兰西”党在年轻人以及族群多元的郊区中拥有强大支持，这些郊区的学校状况最为糟糕。骚乱后进行的民调显示，他的基本盘依然稳固。勒科尔尼指责“不屈法兰西”“利用”抗议活动，并警告极左翼正在利用暴力作为选举的“热身赛”。梅朗雄则将混乱归咎于政府。

不过，真正的受益者是勒庞。她的民调略有上升，目前显示她在总统选举第一轮中的支持率为34%至38%；梅朗雄为15%至20%。10月18日，她发表了一篇总统风格讲话，将暴力归咎于“政治化的打砸分子”和“来自郊区的罪犯”。勒庞认为，这些抗议证明梅朗雄不适合执政，也证明马克龙无法控制国家。一项民调发现，她将在第二轮投票中以68%对32%击败梅朗雄。辩论正在转向法律与秩序，这正中她下怀。

唐纳德·特朗普声称法国正被移民“烧成平地”。但几乎所有的示威者都是法国人，白人的比例与其他任何族裔一样高。一位政府部长暗示存在种族因素——但仅限于抢劫者，称其为“来自郊区的犯罪群体”。这也为外部干预提供了肥沃土壤。美国虚假信息监测机构NewsGuard发现，14条通常将矛头指向移民的虚假报道与一个俄罗斯影响力行动有关。一张巴勒斯坦国旗出现在埃菲尔铁塔塔顶的AI生成图片被浏览了370万次。马克龙表示，确实存在“外部操纵”——不是对事件本身的操纵，而是对事件叙事方式的操纵。

这场暴力有可能使法国偏离其所需要的公共辩论：即法国能负担什么样的福利制度，以及如何创造维持这一制度所需的财富。公共财政状况严峻，债券市场紧张不安。然而中间派分裂，缺乏有吸引力的候选人。而主要政治人物都誓言要降低退休年龄，从而放弃了在最大单一公共支出项目上未来的节省。部分法国人明白这一点。骚乱次日，沉默的选民群体又出现在露台咖啡馆；波尔多一名侍者称这场暴力“可耻”。但激进分子极擅长压制这些声音。除非中间派能够找到一种有说服力的方式，讲述一个负责任的故事，说明公共财政和街头秩序都需要约束，否则选民最终将别无选择，只能在极端之间选择。■

item.title: 失控的抗议撼动阿尔巴尼亚、意大利及其他国家
item.description:
Europe

欧洲 | 一点老派极端暴力 2026年10月22日 在几个欧洲国家，受法国数周抗议活动启发的左翼人士发起了自己的大规模示威。但正如在法国一样，如果此类抗议演变为暴力，很可能有利于右翼。最明显的例子是意大利。10月，中学生开始模仿法国同龄人，占领教室以抗议资金不足。这些行动逐渐发展为反对生活成本上涨的广泛示威，并得到左翼政党和工会的支持。10月17日形势突变，数场游行被黑衣团伙劫持。都灵和博洛尼亚爆发骚乱，米兰大教堂广场被纵火。商店遭抢劫，数十名警察受伤，数百人被捕。一个“10月17日运动”已在Telegram和Instagram上出现，呼吁每周六举行抗议，直到政府下台。一场游行计划于10月2...
item.content:encoded:
失控的抗议撼动阿尔巴尼亚、意大利及其他国家

欧洲 | 一点老派极端暴力 2026年10月22日

在几个欧洲国家，受法国数周抗议活动启发的左翼人士发起了自己的大规模示威。但正如在法国一样，如果此类抗议演变为暴力，很可能有利于右翼。最明显的例子是意大利。10月，中学生开始模仿法国同龄人，占领教室以抗议资金不足。这些行动逐渐发展为反对生活成本上涨的广泛示威，并得到左翼政党和工会的支持。10月17日形势突变，数场游行被黑衣团伙劫持。都灵和博洛尼亚爆发骚乱，米兰大教堂广场被纵火。商店遭抢劫，数十名警察受伤，数百人被捕。一个“10月17日运动”已在Telegram和Instagram上出现，呼吁每周六举行抗议，直到政府下台。一场游行计划于10月24日在罗马举行，许多人预计会发生暴力。骚乱者缺乏明确的领导人，但有一首非官方主题曲：Fabri Fibra的《In Italia 2024》，一首充满社会排斥与反叛的末日色彩颂歌。“我们才刚开始，”来自米兰贫困街区巴罗纳的说唱歌手Marracash表示。许多骚乱者的移民背景为右翼民粹主义政党联盟党领袖马泰奥·萨尔维尼提供了弹药，他呼吁禁止移民在意大利出生的子女在犯罪被定罪后获得公民身份。意大利将于明年举行大选。右翼民粹主义总理焦尔吉娅·梅洛尼已向进步派的民主党及五星运动发起挑战，要求它们谴责暴力。它们若支持合法示威，就可能被视为纵容骚乱。罗马路易斯大学的拉法埃莱·马尔凯蒂表示，对失序的恐惧很可能有利于右翼。10月20日，梅洛尼的内阁批准了对未成年人的预防性拘留，并向米兰的500名士兵授予警务权。然而，骚乱可能对她有利的并非她本人，而是她右翼阵营中的对手。极右翼前将军罗伯托·万纳奇及其反对党“国家未来”表示，警方应使用橡皮子弹和警犬驱散抗议者。其他地方的示威同样呈现左右对立。自9月以来，西班牙人一直在抗议住房成本，并得到社会党首相佩德罗·桑切斯的支持。葡萄牙和希腊也爆发了大规模的生活成本抗议。10月17日，数百名极左活动人士在布鲁塞尔与警方发生冲突。但法国和意大利之外最暴力的示威发生在阿尔巴尼亚，且背景有所不同。自5月31日以来，阿尔巴尼亚人一直在抗议埃迪·拉马总理的政府。数月来抗议活动是和平的；由于唐纳德·特朗普的女婿贾里德·库什纳计划在自然保护区建造海滩度假村，这些抗议被称为“火烈鸟革命”。但自10月13日以来，该运动的一个暴力分支袭击了政府部门、法院、银行和商店。火烈鸟抗议从来不仅仅关乎度假村开发。尽管近年来经济取得进步，阿尔巴尼亚仍是欧洲最贫穷的国家之一，腐败水平很高。拉马声称骚乱受到俄罗斯和伊朗的鼓动。他拒绝辞职，并承诺向警察提供巨额奖金以夺回街头。一位因害怕报复而要求匿名的学者表示，抗议者认为自己能迫使总理下台的想法是错误的，但他的强硬回应已摧毁了他的合法性：“我认为这件事没有回头路了。”大多数抗议者鄙视反对派领袖——他本人曾在1997年因抗议活动而被赶下总统职位。但本周的骚乱可能标志着拉马终结的开始。阿尔巴尼亚、法国、意大利及其他地方的骚乱确实有一个共同点：公民要求的东西，政府无论是因腐败还是财政现实，都无法提供。■

item.title: Europe’s dependence on America in space is hard to escape
item.description:
Europe
